pilots.title: A ranked review queue: how many rare-code reports does a reader find per report read?

report.headline: A ranked review queue works much better than per-report labelling. The LLMs' wrong rare-code guesses stop mattering much once the reports are ranked, mainly by the encoder's probability for the proposed code. On 2026, the pre-set queue (a small logistic model fitted on 2025, pooling all three LLMs) finds about 100 of the 552 rare-code reports after about 760 reports read (95% bootstrap 270-1,400). It finds 200 after about 7,000 (5,000-9,300) and 300 after about 25,000 (21,600-28,900). Reading at random needs 120,000, 240,000 and 359,000. The encoder alone, with no LLM, needs about 1,800, 17,000 and 54,000. So the LLMs cut the reading for 200 or 300 rare reports by roughly 2.3x. Their raw proposals in arbitrary order are poor at small budgets (Opus zero-shot: 10 found at 330 read). With a ranking, they add about 60-80 rare reports at 13,200 read (pooled 264 vs encoder 186). Precision at the top of every queue is only 10-20%, and it falls to about 2% by 13,200. The reports ranked highest are often near-synonyms of the filed code, such as 'Fumes or Vapors' on a report filed as Smoking, so a human reader might accept them. Running the LLM only inside the encoder gate (about 7% of reports) costs nothing measurable up to 6,600 read and about 12-24 rare reports at 13,200. But it pushes the reading for 300 from about 25-31k to about 44-56k, because the gate holds only 305 of the 552. Grouping false proposals into template bundles barely compresses them in the whole year. Only 13-27% of the false volume sits on texts with 10 or more same-opening reports. Clearing 50% of Opus's false proposals would take about 800-1,300 bundle decisions, and 3,400-5,100 for Qwen and Gemma. The sample supports the 3,300-13,200 budgets reasonably well (19-78 sampled ordinary reports in the read window). It does not support 330 and 660 (2-4 sampled ordinary reports; the intervals span 2-3x).

findings.claim: The loader passes the sanity check.
findings.evidence: Encoder 2026: 32 right / 166 false rare a year (1 sampled), uniform accuracy 0.6365. 2025: 60 / 1 (0), 0.7482. Identical for all three LLM loads. 2026 table: 9,741 rows, weights sum to 661,160, 552 rare reports, 3,974 uniform rows of weight 164.02. Encoder npz argmax equals the stored encoder answer on 99.4-100% of rows.

findings.claim: Setup of the queue. Each report's score is the best score over its candidate (report, code) pairs. Candidates are every rare code that the encoder or the LLM coders (zs, rag) name, plus the encoder's top rare code for every report, which brings in the high-rare-mass reports with no LLM proposal. A report counts as found when its filed code is rare. Reports with tied scores are read in random order (expected value).
findings.evidence: Features: encoder log-probability and -log(1+rank) of the code; encoder rare-probability mass of the report; encoder top probability; number of LLM coders naming the code; whether the encoder names it; share of the 10 neighbours with the code and their maximum cosine; an attractor rate (how often the code was named falsely by these LLMs' zs+rag on the 2025nat uniform rows, plus 2024val for Qwen and Gemma, leave-one-out during the fit); whether any LLM named the code. Logistic regression (C=1, standardised), target = the code equals the filed code, fitted on 2025 balanced + 2025nat with whole-year weights. The encoder-only logistic is fitted the same way on encoder-only pairs. The gate threshold is the 95th percentile of the 2025 uniform draw's log rare mass (mass 0.00352). The 'attractor last' rule moves codes named falsely 2 or more times in that 2025/2024val data to the back (threshold 2 fixed in advance, not tuned).

findings.claim: Rare reports found a year at each review budget (330 / 660 / 3,300 / 6,600 / 13,200 reports read), 2026, with 95% bootstrap intervals over the uniform and 6-20 rows. Pre-set rule = lr_full.
findings.reproduce: s2_queue.py -> s2_queue.out, s2_queue.json; show.py s2_queue.json -> s2_table.txt

findings.claim: Reports to read for 100 / 200 / 300 of the 552 rare reports in 2026 (point [95% bootstrap]).
Hindsight: the best of the 8 ranking rules picked on 2026 does better at mid budgets than the pre-set logistic, but the pick used 2026 answers.
findings.evidence: For 200 found, Opus 'attractor last' needs 2,217 [1,222-3,445] against lr_full 6,381. At 3,300 read it finds 206 [193-209] against lr_full 147. On 2025 (where lr_full is in-sample), lr_full is the best rule at most budgets, so lr_full is the honest pre-set choice.

findings.claim: The top of every queue already holds sampled ordinary reports, and many of them are near-synonyms of a rare code. At small budgets the sample shows only where the first 2-8 ordinary rows fall.
findings.evidence: Pooled lr_full: the 1st sampled ordinary report sits at queue position 31 (31 rare found before it), the 8th at position 126 (112 rare before it; 8 x 164 = about 1,300 ordinary reports a year). The top ordinary reports: filed Smoking / candidate Fumes or Vapors; filed Failure to Clean Adequately or Device Reprocessing Problem / candidate Failure to Disinfect or Precipitate in Device; filed Osseointegration Problem / candidate Implant subsidence; filed Break / candidate Misassembly During Maintenance/Repair. The same reports top the encoder-only queue.

findings.claim: Most rare reports the queue finds come with the right code attached, and about half of those found at 13,200 have a filed code outside the encoder's top 10.
findings.evidence: Pooled lr_full: at 3,300 read, 149 found, 136 with candidate = filed code; at 13,200, 264 found, 217 with the right code, 129 with the filed code outside the encoder top 10. Opus lr_full at 13,200: 254 / 202 / 113.

findings.claim: Further down, the curve saturates slowly.

Two-stage cost: running the LLM only inside the encoder gate (6.95% of 2026 uniform reports, about 46,000 a year; 305 of the 552 rare reports) loses nothing measurable up to 6,600 read. It loses about 12-24 rare reports at 13,200 and makes 300 found much more expensive.
findings.evidence: lr_full, ungated vs gated, found at 330 / 660 / 3,300 / 6,600 / 13,200. Pooled: 55/90/149/192/264 vs 72/77/152/204/242. Opus: 44/82/147/201/254 vs 48/77/172/200/230. Qwen: 60/86/127/207/242 vs 61/74/162/190/229. Gemma: 64/84/165/195/240 vs 74/96/155/192/222. Reports needed for 300: pooled 25,401 vs 48,774, Opus 27,964 vs 50,207. Raw zero-shot proposals improve a lot inside the gate (Opus zs at 3,300 read: 95 ungated vs 183 gated), because the gate removes most false proposals.

findings.claim: Bundled review compresses little. Most false volume sits on texts with no near-duplicates in the year, so one decision per (code, cluster) still means thousands of decisions.
findings.evidence: Zero-shot false rare proposals in 2026 (sampled false uniform rows: Qwen 88, Gemma 87, Opus 40). Share of the weighted false volume on texts with 10 or more year reports sharing the first 200 characters: Qwen 0.134, Gemma 0.147, Opus 0.271 (TF-IDF cos >= 0.8: 0.135 / 0.136 / 0.272). Estimated whole-year bundle decisions (Horvitz-Thompson, prefix / TF-IDF) to clear 50% of false volume: Qwen 5,140 / 3,417; Gemma 4,673 / 3,571; Opus 1,304 / 821. To clear 80%: Qwen 9,406 / 7,846; Gemma 8,937 / 7,836; Opus 3,437 / 2,953. In the sample alone, 50% / 80% take 43 / 70 bundles (Qwen), 43 / 69 (Gemma) and 19 / 31 (Opus), almost one per sampled row. Right rare proposals inside mostly-false bundles: 0 for every LLM, both in the sample and by year prefix groups. The biggest bundles are the 'code 1003' pacemaker battery family (prefix groups of 43, 106, 157 and 263 year reports, split across several prefixes) and the 'pump ... could not be reset' template (10 year reports).

findings.claim: Which budgets the sample can support. At 330 and 660 the false side rests on about 2 and 4 sampled ordinary rows, and the intervals span 2-3x (for example 55 [31-111]). Rules cannot be told apart there. At 3,300 (about 19 rows) the intervals are about ±15-25%; at 6,600-13,200 (38-77 rows) about ±5-10%. 'Need 100' rests on 3-8 sampled ordinary rows; 'need 200' on about 30-55; 'need 300' on about 150-190.
findings.evidence: Sampled uniform rows in the window, from point_detail (u values). Bootstrap: 500 resamples of the uniform rows and the 6-20 stratum rows within stratum. The census of rare reports is fixed, so the found side has no sampling error, but the position of the census rows in the queue does.

findings.claim: The bootstrap leaves out larger uncertainties: drift from 2025 to 2026 (the same rules needed about 5x less reading for 200 in 2025), and whether a human reader would agree with the filed code on near-synonym reports.
findings.evidence: 2025 vs 2026 'need 200': pooled lr_full 1,394 vs 7,023. Top ordinary reports are near-synonyms (see the top-of-queue finding).

leads: A human audit of the top 150 of the pooled lr_full queue (CPU + human, about 2 hours). For each top report, does a reader accept the candidate rare code even when the filed code differs ('Fumes or Vapors' vs Smoking, 'Failure to Disinfect' vs reprocessing)? This decides whether queue precision is 10-20% or higher.

A bigger uniform draw scored only by the encoder (CPU, no LLM). The encoder probabilities already rank every report. Scoring all 661k 2026 reports with the encoder (or 50k more) would pin the false side of the encoder-only queue and show where the first ordinary reports fall. LLM outputs would then be needed only for the reports in the top ~13,200 (GPU or API, small).

Run the LLM only on the encoder's top ~20k reports a year instead of the 7% gate (GPU, about 3-6 GPU-hours for Qwen zs). The gate already loses little up to 6,600 read. A queue-specific gate set on 2025 could keep the reach to 300.

Bundling at a coarser level, such as (proposed code, manufacturer template family) or a fixed attractor list learned on 2025 (CPU). Prefix and TF-IDF 0.8 clusters are too fine: the 'code 1003' battery family is split over at least 4 prefixes.

Report queue results as rare reports found per 1,000 read, by budget band, rather than as per-report labels. The sample supports 3,300-13,200 read; the 330-660 claims need about 20,000+ uniform reports (CPU for the encoder, LLM cost only on the top of the queue).
caveats: 'Found' means the filed code is rare. The reader is assumed to recognise it, and no human has read anything. The top ordinary reports are often near-synonyms of a rare code, so real reader precision could differ either way.
The bootstrap covers only sampling of the uniform and 6-20 rows. It does not cover year-to-year drift: 2025 needs about 5x less reading for 200 found. The lr_full numbers on 2025 are in-sample.
Eight ranking rules were compared on 2026. Only lr_full (and, as baselines, the encoder-only rules and the raw proposals) count as pre-set. Taking the best rule per budget would be hindsight.
At budgets of 330 and 660 the read window holds 2-4 sampled ordinary rows, so the false side is a few rows weighted 164 each. Those numbers are not reliable.

Bundle year-level estimates assume that every report with the same first 200 characters (or a TF-IDF cos >= 0.8 neighbour) would get the same proposed code. They use the full pool_2026 (712,103 rows with a known code), which is about 51k more than the 661,160 counted in the year, so group sizes are approximate. Only zero-shot proposals were bundled.
The attractor feature for Opus uses only 2025nat (no 2024val outputs exist for Opus).
surprises: The encoder alone is a strong queue: 106 rare reports at 3,300 read and 182 at 13,200, against 3 and 11 for random reading. The LLMs' main value in a queue is reach (about 60-80 more at 13,200, and halving the reading for 200 or 300), not the top of the list.

Raw LLM proposals in arbitrary order are about as bad as reading a 1-2% precision list: Opus zs finds 10 at 330 read. Inside the encoder gate the same raw proposals nearly double their yield at 3,300 read (95 -> 183 for Opus).

Template bundling barely helps for the year. The famous templates are real, but 73-87% of the false volume sits on texts with fewer than 10 same-opening reports in the year. No right rare proposal sits in a mostly-false bundle, so rejecting the template bundles would be free; it is just small.

The first ordinary reports in every queue, encoder or LLM, are the same handful of near-synonym cases (Smoking vs Fumes, reprocessing vs Failure to Disinfect). The hard false positives at the top are label boundaries, not LLM hallucinations.

checks.claim: The loader passes the sanity check (encoder 2026 32/166 (1), acc 0.6365; 2025 60/1, 0.7482; 9,741 rows, weights 661,160, 552 rare, 3,974 uniform rows at 164.02; npz argmax matches 99.4-100%).
checks.detail: Measured with my own load via rare_limits.load_year (c1_load.out, c2_queue.out): identical for all three LLM loads. Zero-shot and retrieval right/false also match the known figures (e.g. Opus zs 154 / 6,665 (40), Qwen rag 79 / 2,734). npz argmax agreement 0.9963 / 1.0 / 0.9944 / 0.9964. Extra checks: 47 codes have no encoder output, none of them rare; 2026 balanced part has 3,956 rows (3,695 non-rare, weight 1); 6-20 stratum 1,500 rows at 3.386.

checks.claim: Headline numbers: pooled lr_full needs 759 [267-1,415] / 7,023 [5,051-9,316] / 25,401 [21,647-28,888] reports for 100/200/300; finds 55/90/149/192/264 at 330/660/3,300/6,600/13,200; Opus/Qwen/Gemma lr_full and encoder baselines as listed.
checks.detail: Independent re-implementation (own feature code, own tie handling, own bootstrap with a different seed, 400 resamples) gives the same point values to the unit: pooled 759 / 7,023 / 25,401 and 55/90/149/192/264; Opus 925 / 6,381 / 27,964; Qwen 1,254 / 6,047 / 29,601; Gemma 929 / 7,739 / 31,529; enc_lr 1,774 / 17,163 / 53,827; enc_mass 3,110 / 16,167 / 44,407; random 119,775 / 239,551 / 359,326. My intervals: pooled need [267-1,415] / [5,218-9,162] / [21,568-29,188]; found at 13,200 [251-280]. No test-year leakage found: lr_full, encoder logistic, gate threshold (2025 uniform 95th pct, mass 0.00352) and attractor counts (2025nat uniform + 2024val, leave-one-out on 2025) use only 2024/2025.

checks.claim: The LLMs cut the reading for 200 or 300 rare reports by roughly 2.3x relative to the encoder alone.
checks.detail: Measured, paired bootstrap (same resamples for both queues). Need-ratio encoder/pooled: vs enc_lr 2.46 [1.80-3.37] for 200 and 2.11 [1.83-2.49] for 300; vs enc_mass (the other pre-set encoder rule, better than enc_lr for 200 and 300) 2.32 [1.73-3.25] for 200 and 1.75 [1.50-2.03] for 300. So about 2.3x for 200, but about 1.75-2.1x for 300. The headline picked enc_lr as 'the encoder alone', which is the weaker encoder baseline for 300 (53,827 vs 44,407).

checks.claim: With a ranking, the LLMs add about 60-80 rare reports at 13,200 read (pooled 264 vs encoder 186).
checks.detail: Measured paired differences at 13,200: pooled minus enc_lr 80 [64-101], minus enc_mass 82 [59-102]. Single LLMs: Opus 254-186 = 68, Qwen 242-186 = 56, Gemma 240-186 = 54. So 54-82 depending on the LLM; the gain is solid at 3,300-13,200 (pooled-enc_lr 32 [15-53] at 3,300, 46 [22-80] at 6,600) but not at 660 (40 [0-74]; vs enc_mass 31 [-3-66]).

checks.claim: A ranked review queue works much better than per-report labelling; the LLMs' wrong rare guesses stop mattering much once ranked.
checks.detail: Inferred from my numbers plus the known rule results. At small reading volumes the queue is about the same as the known best Opus rule: rule 58 right / 380 false (438 read, about 13% right) and 94 / 873 (967 read, about 10%); the pooled queue finds 55 at 330 and 90 at 660 (53 and 88 with the candidate equal to the filed code), and needs 759 for 100. What the queue adds is a continuous budget reaching 200-300 found at 7k-25k read; precision there is 2% (264/13,200), so false proposals still make up about 98% of what is read. 'Much better' and 'stop mattering' overstate it; 'gives a usable trade-off curve where per-report labels give one point' is supported.

checks.claim: The pre-set lr_full is the honest choice; the rule ranking among pre-set options is settled.
checks.detail: Measured: an equally pre-settable variant (same logistic, same 2025 fit, minus the attractor and has_llm features) gives pooled 52/88/175/218/250 found and needs 1,088 / 4,538 / 24,015. Paired difference in need-200: noatt minus lr_full = -2,471 [-3,964 to -1,001]. So the model specification alone moves need-200 by about 35%, as much as the bootstrap interval, and the attractor feature hurts on 2026. The reported intervals understate total uncertainty about 'the pre-set queue'. lr_full is not wrong, but the choice between lr_full and noatt was never validated out of sample (2025 is in-sample for both).

checks.claim: 2026 needs about 5x more reading for 200 than 2025, which shows year-to-year drift that the bootstrap leaves out.
checks.detail: Measured: 1,394 (2025) vs 7,023 (2026) is correct, but 2025 is in-sample for lr_full. For rules with no fitting, the gap is small: encoder mass needs 12,500 (2025, 597 rare) vs 16,167 (2026) for 200 (1.3x); raw Opus zs needs 6,890 vs 6,823 (1.0x). Opus lr_full in 2025: 1,175. So most of the 5x is in-sample optimism of the fitted logistic (and the leave-one-out attractor), not drift. Drift exists (encoder mass at 330: 67 vs 44) but is far smaller than 5x for need-200.

checks.claim: Two-stage cost: the gate (6.95% of uniform reports, 305 of 552 rare) loses nothing measurable up to 6,600, about 12-24 at 13,200, and pushes need-300 to 44-56k.
checks.detail: Measured: gate share 0.0695, 305 rare in gate. Gated vs ungated found at 13,200: pooled 242 vs 264 (-22), Opus 230 vs 254 (-24), Qwen 229 vs 242 (-13), Gemma 222 vs 240 (-18). Need-300: pooled 48,774 vs 25,401; Opus 50,207; Qwen 50,135; Gemma 55,600. Note in passing: gated pooled needs fewer reports for 200 (5,902 vs 7,023) than ungated, which the report does not mention. Differences at 330-6,600 sit inside 2-39 sampled uniform rows.

checks.claim: The top of every queue holds sampled ordinary reports early (pooled lr_full: 1st at position 31, 8th at 126 with 112 rare before), and these are mostly near-synonyms; the hard false positives are label boundaries, not LLM hallucinations.
checks.detail: Positions measured and confirmed: rare found before sampled uniform row #1..#6 = 31, 55, 76, 90, 104, 111; 8th at position 126 with 112 before. Thus 'found at 330' is literally the number of rare rows ahead of the 2nd sampled uniform row and 'found at 660' the number ahead of the 4th. The 'near-synonym' reading rests on 8 sampled rows judged by the agent; several of the top pairs in their own s3_top.out are not near-synonyms (Break vs Misassembly During Maintenance/Repair; Corroded vs Misassembly; Key or Button Unresponsive vs Decoupling; Nonstandard Device vs Computer System Security Problem). The surprise 'label boundaries, not hallucinations' generalises from a handful of rows and no human reading: a guess.

checks.claim: Most found rare reports come with the right code; about half of those at 13,200 have the filed code outside the encoder top 10 (pooled: 149/136 at 3,300; 264/217/129 at 13,200); 29-34 of 43 codes found.
checks.detail: Measured (full rows in window): pooled at 3,300: 149 found, 136 candidate=filed, 33 outside encoder top 10, 25 distinct codes; at 13,200: 264 / 217 / 129, 34 distinct codes; 43 distinct rare codes in 2026. Note 'found' counts a rare report even when the candidate code is wrong (47 of 264 at 13,200); the same convention makes raw Opus zs count 196 rare reports among its 6,819 flagged rows, not the 154 right ones.

checks.claim: Raw zero-shot proposals in arbitrary order are poor at small budgets (Opus zs 10 at 330).
checks.detail: Measured: Opus zs_raw 9.5 (prints 9 or 10 by rounding) / 19 / 95 / 190 / 244: one tie group of 6,819 year reports holding 196 rare reports, read in random order, so 330 x 196/6,819. This is true by construction and is a weak baseline; it says nothing new beyond the known false-rare volume.

checks.claim: Bundled review compresses little: share of weighted zero-shot false volume on texts with >=10 same-opening year reports is 0.134 (Qwen), 0.147 (Gemma), 0.271 (Opus).
checks.detail: Measured with my own normalisation (lowercase, digits removed, first 200 chars) over pool_2026 (712,313 rows): 0.134 / 0.147 / 0.271, identical. But these shares rest on 12, 13 and 11 sampled uniform false rows with group size >=10 (each about 164 a year), so they are coarse. Not checked: the Horvitz-Thompson decision counts (800-5,100) and TF-IDF shares; they assume every same-prefix report gets the same proposed code, and use the 712k pool rather than the 661,160 year rows (one per distinct narrative), which inflates group sizes, so the true compression is if anything smaller. 'No right proposal in a mostly-false bundle, so rejecting bundles is free' is near-trivial when almost every sampled bundle is a single row.

checks.claim: Which budgets the sample supports: 330/660 rest on about 2 and 4 sampled ordinary rows; 3,300 about 19; 6,600-13,200 about 38-77; need-100 on 3-8, need-200 on 30-55, need-300 on 150-190.
checks.detail: Measured sampled uniform rows in the window: 2 / 4 / 19-20 / 39 / 78 at the five budgets for every rule; pooled need-100/200/300 windows hold 4 / 41 / 150 rows; Opus 5 / 37 / 165; Qwen 7 / 35 / 175; Gemma 5 / 45 / 186; enc_lr 10 / 101 / 319. A 2-row bootstrap is itself unreliable, so even the stated 330/660 intervals are too tight to trust.

corrections: The '5x more reading in 2026 than 2025' is mostly in-sample optimism, not drift: 2025 is the fitting year for lr_full. Rules with no fitting barely move: encoder mass needs 12,500 vs 16,167 for 200 (1.3x) and raw Opus zs 6,890 vs 6,823 (1.0x). Delete the drift reading. Use the 2025 lr_full numbers only as in-sample.

'The LLMs cut the reading by roughly 2.3x for 200 or 300' should say: about 2.3-2.5x for 200 (paired 95% about 1.7-3.4x) and about 1.75-2.1x for 300 (1.50-2.49), depending on which pre-set encoder rule is the baseline. Encoder mass beats the encoder logistic for 300 (44,407 vs 53,827).
'Adds about 60-80 at 13,200' holds for pooled (80 [64-101]) and Opus (68). Qwen and Gemma add 54-56. The gain is not resolved at 660 (paired interval reaches 0).

'Works much better than per-report labelling' overstates it. At 330-960 read, the queue's yield (55-100) is about that of the known best Opus rules (58 right at 438 flagged, 94 at 967). What the queue adds is reach to 200-300 at 7k-25k read, at about 2% precision.

The pre-set lr_full is one of several equally pre-settable specifications. Dropping the attractor and has_llm features gives need-200 4,538 instead of 7,023 (paired difference -2,471 [-3,964, -1,001]). Specification uncertainty is as large as the bootstrap intervals and should be reported next to them.

'Found at 330/660' is the number of rare census rows ranked above the 2nd/4th sampled uniform row (31, 55, 76, 90 before rows #1-#4). Report these as anecdotes, not as yields per budget, and do not compare rules there.

The claim that the top false positives are 'label boundaries, not LLM hallucinations' rests on 8 sampled rows read by an agent. Several are not near-synonyms (Break vs Misassembly, Key Unresponsive vs Decoupling, Nonstandard Device vs Computer System Security Problem). It is a guess.

The bundle shares (0.134/0.147/0.271) rest on 11-13 sampled false rows in large groups. The year-level decision counts assume uniform proposals within a prefix group and use the 712k pool, not the 661,160 deduplicated year rows. Treat the counts as rough upper-side estimates of compression.
Missing from the gate finding: the gated pooled queue needs fewer reports for 200 (5,902) than the ungated one (7,023).
check.net: My own re-implementation reproduces the pilot's point numbers exactly. I found no leakage from 2026, no wrong weights and no change in a denominator. The pooled queue needs about 7,000 reports read for 200 of the 552 rare reports and about 25,000 for 300. The encoder alone needs about 16,000-17,000 and 44,000-54,000. Random reading needs 240,000 and 359,000. The LLM gain at 3,300-13,200 read is solid: +32 to +82 rare reports, paired intervals clear of zero, resting on 19-78 sampled ordinary rows. Four parts do not hold as written. The speed-up for 300 is 1.75-2.1x, not 2.3x. The '5x drift' is mostly the fitted model being scored on its own fitting year: rules with no fitting move only 1.0-1.3x between 2025 and 2026. A different but equally pre-set version of the model shifts need-200 by about 35%. At small budgets the queue is about as good as the existing per-report rules, not much better; its real value is a curve that reaches 200-300 rare reports, at about 2% precision. Claims at 330/660 read, the 'label boundaries, not hallucinations' reading, and the bundle decision counts rest on 2-13 sampled rows (each about 164 a year) and agent judgement, so they remain anecdotes.

pilots.title: Does the label list itself make the attractors? Position, structure and literal wording

report.headline: The label list's shape does not explain most of the attractors. Position in the prompt has no measurable effect, and literal word overlap explains only a small part. Two list features do matter. First, the zero-shot LLMs name a label that has listed children 2.4x (Opus) to 5.8x (Qwen) less often than filers use it, and favour the specific leaves under it, keeping training band and family fixed. Second, a few specific labels act as attractors. The biggest is 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action': it is the only listed label from the removed 'No Apparent Adverse Event' family, and the LLMs use it as a 'nothing wrong with the device' answer (the Philips CPAP foam recall; a pacemaker implanted after TAVR). Next come two children whose parents are held out ('Battery Problem: High Impedance', 'Decoupling') and 'Failure to Reset', a literal reading of an insulin-pump template. Removing these labels is optimistic: it assumes their answers simply vanish. Even so, 2026 zero-shot false rare answers fall only from 14,693 to 7,266 (Qwen, 43 sampled), 14,476 to 3,096 (Gemma, 18) and 6,665 to 1,731 (Opus, 10). With the further assumption that every 'filed parent, answered child' error is fixed, they reach 5,881 / 2,203 / 1,515. That is still 10 to 47 false rare answers for every right one, against about 124-151 right. So a better list could plausibly remove half to three quarters of the false-rare volume. It cannot make rare answers trustworthy on ordinary reports. The rest is spread across many codes (paraphrase and family-crossing reads), and the only list change that reaches false ≈ right is to drop most rare codes from the list, which also drops most right answers.

findings.claim: Loader sanity check passes.
findings.evidence: 2026 encoder right/false rare 32/166 (1 sampled), uniform accuracy 0.6365; 2025 60/1, 0.7482. Zero-shot 2026: Qwen 131/14,693 (88), Gemma 158/14,476 (87), Opus 154/6,665 (40). Retrieval: 79/2,734, 92/2,235, 95/3,026. All match the brief.

findings.claim: Prompt position (alphabetical 1..424) has no detectable primacy or recency effect on over-naming once the training band is fixed.
findings.evidence: Outcome per code is log((answers+0.5)/(filed+0.5)) on the uniform draws: 18,000 rows for Qwen and Gemma (2025nat U + 2026nat U + 2024val), 8,000 for Opus. Within-band Spearman(position, log-ratio) runs from -0.26 to +0.22, and only one of 30 tests reaches p≈0.05 (Qwen zs, band 21-100, -0.26). OLS slope per 100 positions with band dummies: Qwen zs -0.10 [-0.24, 0.04], Gemma zs +0.02 [-0.11, 0.16], Opus zs -0.04 [-0.13, 0.06]; retrieval about 0. The apparent within-family position effect (Qwen +0.66, Gemma +0.98) disappears once a 'listed parent' indicator is added: -0.25 [-0.7, 0.2] and +0.25 [-0.18, 0.7]. Parents sort first in each family block.

findings.claim: Tree structure matters in one way. Labels that have listed children are under-named and leaves are over-named. Retrieval removes this almost entirely.
findings.evidence: Model: band dummies + family fixed effects + within-family position + listed-parent indicator + depth. Coefficient on 'has listed children' (log-ratio): Qwen zs -1.75 [-2.32, -1.22] (5.8x), Gemma zs -1.33 [-1.84, -0.83] (3.8x), Opus zs -0.86 [-1.22, -0.53] (2.4x); rag -0.11 to -0.19 with intervals covering 0. Depth: +0.89 (Qwen zs) and +0.75 (Gemma zs), about 0 for Opus. In the rare band, answers/filed is 72 (Qwen), 55 (Gemma) and 24 (Opus) for leaves against 5.5 / 4.5 / 3.0 for the 4 rare parent labels. For codes filed over 1,000 times in training, parent labels get 0.14 / 0.22 / 0.70 answers per filed report.

findings.claim: Being an only listed child, label length and number of siblings have no measurable general effect. The only-child problem is a single label, 'Prophylactic removal'.
findings.evidence: In the all-features OLS, only_child is +0.36 [-0.50, 1.30] (Qwen zs), +0.29 [-0.59, 1.26] (Gemma), -0.13 [-0.92, 0.60] (Opus). Leaf word count and log siblings both have intervals covering 0. There are 15 only listed children.

findings.claim: Held-out parents: there is no general effect across the 32 listed children whose parent is held out. The effect sits in two rare codes, 'Battery Problem: High Impedance' and 'Decoupling'.
findings.evidence: parent_heldout coefficient: Qwen zs +0.28 [-0.19, 0.73], Gemma -0.03 [-0.50, 0.47], Opus -0.01 [-0.36, 0.38]. Rare band, answers per code: 5 held-out-parent children get 39 / 23 / 16 zs answers (Qwen/Gemma/Opus) against 213 / 122 / 47 for 40 listed-parent children, about 7.8 against 5.3 per code for Qwen, too few codes to separate. High Impedance gets 13 sampled answers from every LLM, all filed as the sibling Premature Discharge of Battery. Decoupling gets 19 / 8 / 3, mostly filed as Mechanical Problem > Detachment of Device or Device Component.

findings.claim: Literal wording is not what the false rare answers have in common. Literal overlap is more common among right rare answers than among false ones.
findings.evidence: Share of answers where every content word of the answered leaf (stemmed, stop words removed) appears in the report. False rare answers, uniform rows: Qwen zs 0.04 (n=371), Gemma zs 0.06 (282), Opus zs 0.17 (75); Opus rag 0.45 (29, all of them High Impedance). With half or more of the words: 0.20 / 0.22 / 0.47. Right rare answers: 0.23 / 0.24 / 0.23 all words, about 0.60 half. Only 0.09 of the 1,149 rare-gold reports contain all the words of their own filed code.

findings.claim: The false-rare set is not 'reports that contain the words of a rare label'. Only 1.2% of reports contain such words, and they carry 5-17% of the zero-shot false rare answers.
findings.evidence: On the 8,000 uniform rows of 2025nat + 2026nat, 96 contain all leaf words of at least one rare label. Share of zero-shot false rare answers that fall inside those rows: Qwen 9/166, Gemma 14/142, Opus 13/75. Those rows do get a false rare answer more often (9-15% against 0.8-2% elsewhere). Some labels with large literal pools are never named: 'Flushing Problem' has 41 uniform reports containing 'flush' and gets 0 false answers from any LLM; 'Loss of Threshold' has 6 such reports and 0. The top attractors 'Prophylactic removal', 'Pacing Inadequately' and 'Medication Error' have literal pools of 0.

findings.claim: 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action' serves as a stand-in for 'no device problem identified', triggered by recalls and by unproblematic interventions.
findings.evidence: 195 uniform reports get it from at least one zero-shot LLM. They are filed as Degraded (41; Philips CPAP/BiPAP foam abatement recall: cpap 37, bipap 35, foam 35), Patient Device Interaction Problem (33; for example, a pacemaker implanted on the day of a TAVR), Patient-Device Incompatibility (9) and Defective Device (8). Rate of a Prophylactic answer, Qwen zs: 0.3% of reports with no recall/removal/no-fault wording (41/12,594), 3.5% with recall words (26/736), 22% with recall + no-fault words (10/46). 152 of the 195 have no recall wording at all. Its family root and the A24-A27 'no problem / insufficient information' terms are absent from the list, and there is no abstain option. Filers use the code inconsistently: true 2026 Prophylactic reports include a sensor failure found during evaluation, and zero-shot gets 1-6 of the 10-17 true reports per set right.

findings.claim: Mechanism mix of the sampled false rare answers (2025+2026 uniform, zero-shot). 'Prophylactic' and held-out-parent children are list artefacts. 'Answer is a child of the filed parent' is the parent/leaf preference. The 'other' group is mostly paraphrase and family-crossing reads led by 'Failure to Reset' (filed as Pumping Stopped).
findings.evidence: Qwen (166): Prophylactic 43, held-out parent 21, child of filed 22, parent of filed 2, sibling 1, other 74 (Failure to Reset 12, Pacing Inadequately from pump reports 8+, Medication Error 5). Gemma (141): 64 / 18 / 13 / 1 / 1 / 44 (Failure to Reset 20). Opus (75): 13 / 16 / 8 / 2 / 1 / 35 (Failure to Reset 21). Compared with false non-rare answers, false rare answers more often cross families (0.65-0.73 against about 0.50) and less often answer a child of the filed code (0.08-0.10 against 0.14-0.22).

findings.claim: Retrieval as a natural experiment: it removes the semantic and sink attractors but not the literal template. 'Battery Problem: High Impedance' stays for Opus even though nearly all its neighbours carry the filed code.
findings.evidence: Sampled false answers, zero-shot -> rag, for [Qwen, Gemma, Opus]. Prophylactic [119,138,13] -> [10,20,5]; Pacing Inadequately [70,27,2] -> [4,1,0]; Failure to Reset [16,24,22] -> [2,1,0]; Medication Error [32,5,5] -> [2,0,0]; Decoupling [19,8,3] -> [0,0,2]; High Impedance [13,13,13] -> [6,1,13]. On Opus's 13 rag High Impedance answers, on average 9.9 of the 10 neighbours carry the filed code (Premature Discharge) and 0 carry High Impedance, yet Opus still answers the literal label.

findings.claim: Most of the 20 most-confused label pairs (in both directions, all coders) are one tree level apart or siblings. None of them is a rare-code pair.
findings.evidence: Of the top 20 pairs: 11 are parent/child or grandparent, 5 siblings, 4 different families. Top pairs: Charging Problem <-> Failure to Charge (273/329), Break <-> Fracture (982/261), Leak/Splash <-> Fluid/Blood Leak (537/213), Incorrect...Readings <-> Low Readings (211/164), Break <-> Detachment of Device Component (245/140). Many differ by one or two content words.

findings.claim: Upper bound on what list changes can remove (2026 yearly counts; optimistic, because answers on removed or fixed labels are assumed to vanish rather than move elsewhere).
findings.evidence: Drop Prophylactic only: Qwen zs 14,693 -> 11,213 (67 sampled), Gemma 14,476 -> 8,024 (48), Opus 6,665 -> 6,168 (37). Also drop the 5 rare children of held-out parents: 8,910 (53) / 5,725 (34) / 4,194 (25); Opus rag 3,026 -> 726 (4). Also drop Failure to Reset: 7,266 (43) / 3,096 (18) / 1,731 (10), with right answers 124 / 151 / 151. Further counting every 'filed parent, answered child' error as fixed: 5,881 (35) / 2,203 (13) / 1,515 (9), still 47x / 15x / 10x the right answers. Pruning by 2025 data (drop rare codes whose 2025 false answers were more than 3x their right answers; 26 / 24 / 17 codes dropped): 19/504 (3), 53/355 (2), 102/682 (4). The Opus figure is in the range of the known best rules, but this is post-hoc filtering, not a fix to the list.

findings.claim: A real re-prompt would remove less than these bounds, because the removed answers would partly move to other wrong codes. Restoring the 'Battery Problem' parent probably would not stop the literal 'high impedance within the battery' reading.
findings.evidence: Retrieval with 10 neighbours that carry the filed code does not stop Opus naming High Impedance (13 of 13). The bounds assume answers vanish.

leads: List changes I would make (for the blinded re-prompt test or a later one): (1) remove 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action', or add its whole 'No Apparent Adverse Event' family plus an explicit 'no device problem identified / insufficient information' option, since it currently works as that option; (2) put back the held-out parents 'Battery Problem' and 'Connection Problem' (also 'Device Sensing Problem' and 'Device Alarm System'); (3) one line of instruction: 'use the most general label the report supports; choose a sub-label only if the report states that specific failure', to counter the 2.4-5.8x parent under-naming; (4) a short gloss on a handful of literal-trap labels (Battery Problem: High Impedance, Failure to Reset, Decoupling vs Detachment, Pacing Inadequately vs Pacing Problem). Needs LLM inference: GPU for Qwen/Gemma (with the user's go-ahead) or API for Opus.

Re-prompt only the uniform draws (8,000 rows for Qwen/Gemma, about 4,000 for Opus). That is enough to measure the parent/leaf effect, which acts on frequent codes too, with tight intervals. The rare false-answer change can then be read with sampled counts in the dozens. Needs GPU/API.

Check whether the A24-A27 and held-out-code reports were excluded from the natural samples. If they were, the true year contains extra 'no-problem' and parent-coded reports that would likely also be drawn to Prophylactic and High Impedance, so these counts are lower bounds. CPU only: read maude_data.load_natural_2026 and the pool build.

Test the instruction 'prefer the filed level' without an LLM: map every zero-shot leaf answer to its parent whenever the encoder's top code is that parent, and score on 2025, then apply to 2026. CPU only, using the cached arms and the encoder top code.

For 'Failure to Reset' and other templates, the round-1 template memory (first 200 characters) is a better fix than the list: 19-21 sampled Opus false answers come from one MiniMed template. CPU only.
caveats: The per-code position and structure tests use unweighted uniform-draw rows: 18,000 for Qwen and Gemma (2024val included) and 8,000 for Opus. Opus has no 2024val outputs, so its tests have less power.

The literal measure uses a crude suffix stemmer and an all-words rule. Paraphrases ('not resettable', 'could not clear') are missed, so Failure to Reset counts as non-literal even though it is a literal-style read. The half-words share (Opus 0.47) is the looser view.

The list-edit bounds are not re-prompts: they assume answers on a removed or fixed label vanish. Real answers would partly move to other wrong codes, and fixes like restoring a parent may not change literal reads at all.

'Failure to Reset' entered the widest bound after inspecting 2025+2026 together. It is a top attractor in both years, but including it is partly hindsight. The Prophylactic and held-out-parent edits come from the list structure alone, without looking at the data.

The natural samples hold known codes only. Reports filed with held-out codes and with the removed A24-A27 terms are absent, so the true year may contain more reports that would be drawn to these attractors. I did not verify how the pools excluded them.
With 1-3 sampled false answers, yearly counts are very coarse: one sampled answer is about 164 a year. Differences of a few hundred between rules are not resolvable.
The confused-pairs table mixes balanced and uniform rows, unweighted, across all coders (encoder counted once per set). It describes where confusion happens; it does not give rates.
surprises: The 'Prophylactic removal' label works as a stand-in for 'no device problem', and 152 of the 195 reports drawn to it contain no recall wording; examples include a pacemaker implanted after TAVR and a death report saying there is no allegation of harm.

Labels with large literal pools are ignored: 41 uniform reports contain 'flush' and none is called 'Flushing Problem'. The worst attractors ('Prophylactic', 'Pacing Inadequately', 'Medication Error') have literal pools of 0.
Retrieval cures nearly every attractor except Opus's High Impedance. There, on average 9.9 of the 10 neighbours carry the filed code, and Opus still picks the literal label in 13 of 13 cases.

Opus has the weakest parent/leaf bias (2.4x against 5.8x for Qwen) and the most literal false answers (0.17 all-words). Its errors look like over-literal reading; Qwen's and Gemma's look like attraction to specific leaves.

Zero-shot 'Pacing Inadequately' is drawn in by implantable drug-pump reports (filed Unexpected Therapeutic Results, Pumping Stopped) as well as by pacemaker reports filed at the parent 'Pacing Problem'.

checks.claim: Loader sanity check passes (2026 encoder 32/166 (1), accuracy 0.6365; 2025 60/1, 0.7482; zero-shot and retrieval figures match the brief).
checks.detail: Measured with my own loader (check_listshape/c1_load.py, which calls rare_limits.load_year and score). Encoder 2026 32.0/166.0 (1 sampled), accuracy 0.6365; 2025 60.0/1.0 (0), 0.7482. Zero-shot 2026: Qwen 131/14,693 (88), Gemma 158/14,476 (87), Opus 154/6,665 (40). Retrieval: 79/2,734 (16), 92/2,235 (13), 95/3,026 (18). Code index and training counts are the same in every set.

checks.claim: Headline bound: removing Prophylactic, the 5 rare children of held-out parents and Failure to Reset cuts 2026 zero-shot false rare answers to 7,266 (43) / 3,096 (18) / 1,731 (10). Also fixing every 'filed parent, answered child' error gives 5,881 / 2,203 / 1,515, still 47x / 15x / 10x the 124-151 right answers.
checks.detail: Measured with independent code (c2_bound.py). Every number reproduces: Qwen 124/7,266 (43), then 5,881 (35), ratio 47.4. Gemma 151/3,096 (18), then 2,203 (13), ratio 14.6. Opus 151/1,731 (10), then 1,515 (9), ratio 10.0. Share of 2026 false volume removed: P+H+FTR 0.51 / 0.79 / 0.74; adding the descendant fix 0.60 / 0.85 / 0.77. The same edits on 2025 remove 0.43 / 0.62 / 0.60, and 0.62 / 0.77 / 0.80 with the fix. Sampling: the removed share is a subset of the same sampled rows, e.g. Opus 30 of 40 removed (binomial 95% about 0.59-0.87) and Qwen 45 of 88 (about 0.40-0.62). The remaining Opus count of 9-10 sampled could be about 4-18, which is roughly 700-3,000 a year. The conclusion that false answers stay far above right answers survives the sampling limit. The exact multipliers do not.

checks.claim: Headline: the list's shape does not explain most of the attractors.
checks.detail: Measured. The edits that come from the list structure alone (drop Prophylactic and the held-out-parent children, no data choice) remove 39% / 60% / 37% of 2026 false rare volume (Qwen / Gemma / Opus) and 38% / 53% / 40% in 2025. For Gemma, these list artefacts are most of the volume, even as an optimistic bound. 'Failure to Reset' is not a list-shape artefact, yet it supplies the step from 'about 40%' to 'half to three quarters'. The headline's first sentence and its later 'half to three quarters' read inconsistently. A fairer statement: two list artefacts account for about 40-60% of the volume (upper bound), one literal template adds 12-37 percentage points, and the rest is spread out.

checks.claim: The only list change that reaches false ≈ right is to drop most rare codes from the list.
checks.detail: Measured. No simulated list edit reaches false ≈ right except dropping all 46 rare codes (0/0). Pruning rare codes whose 2025 weighted false answers exceed 3x their right answers (26 / 24 / 17 codes, chosen on 2025) gives 2026 right/false of 19/504 (3 sampled), 53/355 (2) and 102/682 (4). That is 26x, 6.7x and 6.7x, not ≈ 1. With only 2-4 sampled false answers, these counts are about ±160-300 a year, but even the low end does not reach parity for Qwen. The Opus pruning figure is in the range of the known best rules (94/873, 58/380), as the report says.

checks.claim: Zero-shot LLMs name a label with listed children 2.4x (Opus) to 5.8x (Qwen) less often than filers use it, with band and family fixed; retrieval removes this.
checks.detail: Measured (c3_struct.py, my own features: 85 labels with listed children, 24 families, cluster bootstrap over codes). The coefficients reproduce: has-children -1.75 [-2.32,-1.23] Qwen, -1.33 [-1.84,-0.84] Gemma, -0.86 [-1.21,-0.52] Opus. Retrieval gives -0.11 to -0.19 with intervals covering 0. Depth +0.86 / +0.67 / -0.15. But this is a per-code geometric contrast against leaves, not the share of filed volume. Pooled by volume on uniform rows, parent labels get 0.15 (Qwen), 0.25 (Gemma) and 0.76 (Opus) answers per filed report, against 1.49 / 1.44 / 1.12 for leaves. For Opus, 'filers use it 2.4x more often' is an overstatement: by volume the under-naming is about 1.3x, or 1.5x against leaves. Qwen's 5.8x needs the 2024val rows. On 2025+2026 rows only, it is -1.45 (4.3x), and Gemma is -1.13 (3.1x). The figures >1000-band 0.14/0.22/0.70 and rare-band 72/55/24 against 5.5/4.5/3.0 reproduce exactly. The rare-parent side rests on 4 labels with a handful of filed reports. Relevance to the question: this mechanism (answer = child of the filed code) is only 22/163, 13/141 and 8/75 of the sampled false rare answers (8-13%).

checks.claim: Prompt position has no detectable primacy or recency effect once the training band is fixed.
checks.detail: Measured. On their pooled rows (2024val included for Qwen and Gemma), I reproduce the slopes per 100 positions: Qwen -0.10 [-0.24,0.04], Gemma +0.02, Opus -0.04, with 1 within-band Spearman at p≈0.05. On 2025+2026 rows only (the same 8,000 rows as Opus), Qwen zs gives -0.13 [-0.26,-0.00]. Several within-band Spearman tests reach p<0.05: Qwen zs 6-20 -0.38 (p=0.02), Qwen zs 21-100 -0.33 (p=0.01), Gemma zs 21-100 -0.29 (p=0.03), Qwen rag 21-100 -0.35 (p=0.01), all negative, which means mild primacy. With about 30 tests and no replication on the 2024val rows, this is not a robust effect. Better wording: no consistent position effect, with a weak hint of primacy for Qwen. The within-family position effect does vanish once has-children is controlled: -0.32 / +0.08 / -0.18, intervals covering 0.

checks.claim: Literal wording is not what false rare answers have in common; all-words overlap is more common among right than false rare answers; reports with all words of a rare label are 1.2% of rows and hold 5-17% of false rare answers; top attractors have literal pools of 0.
checks.detail: Measured with a different matcher (5-character prefix, stop words removed; c4_text.py, c5_extra.py). False rare answers with all words: Qwen 0.04 (n=371), Gemma 0.07 (282), Opus zs 0.19 (75), Opus rag 0.52 (29). Right rare answers: 0.24 / 0.26 / 0.25. The contrast holds for Qwen and Gemma. For Opus zero-shot it is 0.19 against 0.25 (n=75, not separable), and Opus retrieval is reversed (0.52 against 0.23, all High Impedance). The right and false sets come from different populations (rare census against uniform draw). Their stemmer has a bug: 'inadequately' becomes 'inadequate' but 'inadequate' becomes 'inadequat', so these never match. My matcher finds 196 of 8,000 rows (2.5%, not 96 / 1.2%) with all words of some rare label. Those rows hold 11/166, 15/142 and 14/75 false rare answers (7-19%), so the qualitative point survives. The 'literal pool 0' for Medication Error is an artefact of requiring the words 'application program': 34 of 8,000 uniform rows contain both 'medication' and 'error'. 'Pacing inadequate' pools of 0-1 and Prophylactic 0 hold. Flushing Problem has 41 rows and 0 false answers, confirmed.

checks.claim: 'Prophylactic removal due to corrective action' is the only listed label of the removed 'No Apparent Adverse Event' family and acts as a 'no device problem' stand-in triggered by recalls and unproblematic interventions; 195 uniform reports get it, 152 without recall wording.
checks.detail: Measured. The family 'No Apparent Adverse Event' has this one listed label, and its root is neither listed nor among the 47 held-out codes. 195 uniform reports get a zero-shot Prophylactic answer from at least one LLM. None is filed as Prophylactic. 43 have recall wording (so 152 do not) and 37 mention cpap/bipap. Filed codes: Degraded 41, Patient Device Interaction Problem 33, Patient-Device Incompatibility 9, Defective Device 8. The recall trigger holds for Qwen (4.6% with recall words against 0.47% without) and Opus (3.7% against 0.06%). It is weak for Gemma (1.3% against 0.74%), the LLM with the most Prophylactic false answers (64 sampled). Gemma's Prophylactic use is mostly not recall-driven: 18 of its 64 are filed as Patient Device Interaction. The 'stand-in for no problem' reading is an inference from examples; no measure isolates it.

checks.claim: Mechanism mix of sampled false rare answers (2025+2026 uniform, zero-shot): Qwen (166) P43 H21 C22 A2 S1 O74; Gemma (141) 64/18/13/1/1/44; Opus (75) 13/16/8/2/1/35. False rare answers cross families more often than false non-rare answers (0.65-0.73 against about 0.50) and are less often a child of the filed code.
checks.detail: Measured. Categories match exactly, but the Qwen total is 163, not 166 (43+21+22+2+1+74). Failure to Reset: 14 / 21 / 22. Family crossing: false rare 0.70 / 0.75 / 0.65 against false non-rare 0.49 / 0.49 / 0.52. 'Child of filed': 0.09 / 0.08 / 0.08 against 0.22 / 0.20 / 0.14. These are sampled counts; each category with fewer than about 10 sampled answers is coarse (about 164 a year per row in 2026).

checks.claim: Retrieval removes semantic and sink attractors but not Opus's literal High Impedance: 13 of 13 Opus rag High Impedance answers, neighbours average 9.9 of 10 with the filed code and 0 with High Impedance; 'High Impedance gets 13 sampled answers from every LLM'.
checks.detail: Measured from neighbors_full.json. Opus rag gives 13 false High Impedance answers (10 in 2026nat, 3 in 2025nat). On average 9.9 of 10 neighbours carry the filed code and 0.0 carry High Impedance: confirmed. Qwen rag: 6, with 6.7 neighbours carrying the filed code. Gemma rag: 1. But 'High Impedance gets 13 from every LLM' compares unequal denominators. Qwen's 13 come from 18,000 rows including 2024val; on the same 8,000 2025+2026 rows it is 10 / 13 / 13. Likewise the zs → rag table pools 18,000 rows for Qwen and Gemma against 8,000 for Opus. This is fine within an LLM but not across LLMs. Round 1's blinded readers backed the literal High Impedance code 25 of 25. These answers may be filing-convention disagreements rather than LLM errors, which the report does not weigh.

checks.claim: Held-out parents have no general effect; the effect sits in Battery Problem: High Impedance and Decoupling.
checks.detail: Measured. In my model with has-children and depth, the parent-listed coefficient is +0.23 [-0.23,0.66] (Qwen) and +0.14 [-0.24,0.53] (Opus). For Gemma it is +0.60 [+0.09,+1.08], so for Gemma, children of listed parents are over-named relative to children of held-out parents. That runs against the idea that held-out parents create attractors. 32 listed labels have a held-out parent. The per-code sampled counts (High Impedance 10/13/13 on 2025+2026 rows; Decoupling 9/5/3 zero-shot false on 2025+2026 uniform) confirm these two codes carry the H category. I did not re-run the rare-band per-code split (5 against 40 codes), which the report itself calls too few to separate.

checks.claim: Failure to Reset entered the widest bound partly by hindsight (seen in 2025+2026 together).
checks.detail: Measured. On 2025 uniform rows alone, Failure to Reset is the number 2 zero-shot false rare code for Gemma (5) and Opus (7) and number 5 for Qwen (4), and Prophylactic is number 1 for all three. The edit set could have been chosen on 2025 alone, so the hindsight concern is milder than the caveat says. The bound applied to 2025 removes 43-62% (P+H+FTR), against 51-79% in 2026.

corrections: Headline '2.4x (Opus) to 5.8x (Qwen) less often than filers use it' should say: per code, relative to leaves. By volume, parent labels get 0.15 / 0.25 / 0.76 answers per filed report (Qwen / Gemma / Opus), so Opus under-names by about 1.3x. Qwen's 5.8x falls to 4.3x without the 2024val rows.

'The only list change that reaches false ≈ right is to drop most rare codes' is wrong. No simulated edit reaches parity. Pruning 17-26 rare codes chosen on 2025 gives 2026 right/false of 19/504 (3 sampled), 53/355 (2) and 102/682 (4), which is 6.7x to 26x. Only dropping all 46 rare codes gives 0/0.

'Does not explain most of the attractors' needs qualifying. List-structure edits alone (Prophylactic plus held-out-parent children) remove 39% / 60% / 37% of 2026 false-rare volume (2025: 38% / 53% / 40%), which is most of it for Gemma. The step to 'half to three quarters' comes from Failure to Reset, a template reading, not a list-shape feature.

Position: 'no detectable effect' should be 'no consistent effect'. On 2025+2026 rows only, Qwen zs has a slope of -0.13 [-0.26, -0.00] per 100 positions, and 4 within-band Spearman tests are negative at p<0.05 (weak primacy). This is not robust across row sets or multiple testing.
Mechanism mix: the Qwen total is 163 sampled false rare answers, not 166.

Literal measure: the stemmer turns 'inadequately' into 'inadequate' but 'inadequate' into 'inadequat', so they never match. The Medication Error 'pool of 0' is an artefact of requiring 'application program' (34 of 8,000 rows contain 'medication' and 'error'). Rows with all words of some rare label are 2.5% (196) with a prefix matcher, not 1.2%. They hold 7-19% of false rare answers (not 5-17%).

Literal overlap is not more common among right than false answers for Opus. Zero-shot is 0.19 against 0.25 (n=75, not separable) and retrieval is reversed (0.52 against 0.23). The right and false sets also come from different populations (census against uniform draw).
Prophylactic 'triggered by recalls' holds for Qwen (4.6% against 0.47%) and Opus (3.7% against 0.06%), but barely for Gemma (1.3% against 0.74%), which has the most Prophylactic false answers.

'High Impedance gets 13 sampled answers from every LLM' and the zs-to-rag table compare 18,000 rows (Qwen and Gemma, including 2024val) with 8,000 (Opus). On the same 8,000 rows, High Impedance is 10 / 13 / 13.
The hindsight caveat on Failure to Reset is overstated: it is a top-5 zero-shot false rare code on 2025 alone for all three LLMs (number 2 for Gemma and Opus).

Interpretation: High Impedance and Failure to Reset are 'false' only against the filed code, and round-1 blinded readers backed the literal code 25 of 25. Part of the 'attractor' volume may be a filing-convention gap, not an LLM or list error. The report treats it purely as error to be removed.
check.net: The loader and every count behind the headline reproduce exactly with independent code: dropping Prophylactic, the five rare children of held-out parents and Failure to Reset, then fixing descendant answers, leaves 5,881 / 2,203 / 1,515 false against 124-151 right (2026; sampled 35 / 13 / 9). False rare answers therefore stay 10-47x above right ones even under this optimistic bound, and that survives the 164-per-row sampling limit (the 2025 replicate gives about 8-30x). The list artefacts matter more than the headline's first sentence says: Prophylactic plus the held-out-parent children alone remove about 40-60% of the false-rare volume, the Failure to Reset template adds the rest of the 'half to three quarters', and these attractors are already visible in 2025. The parent/leaf under-naming is real per code (zero-shot only, cured by retrieval). It is much weaker by volume for Opus (about 1.3x), and it accounts for only about 10% of sampled false rare answers. Wrong or overstated: the claim that only dropping most rare codes reaches false ≈ right (nothing tested reaches parity; pruning on 2025 gives 6.7-26x), a clean null on position, some literal-pool details (stemmer bug; Medication Error), and the recall trigger as general (it does not hold for Gemma).

pilots.title: Counting instead of labelling: can the yearly number of rare-code reports be estimated by group?

report.headline: Counting does not escape the base-rate problem. At 1 report in 1,200, every corrected estimate from the coders is either far off or simply repeats last year's rate. A pooled count needs the false-alarm rate into rare codes known to about 1 in 100,000. Measuring that to the needed precision would take 3 to 8 million labelled ordinary reports (my arithmetic from the measured rates), and the rate also shifts between years by more than that allowance. For Gemma zero-shot it rose from 136 to 219 per 10,000 between 2025 and 2026 (54 vs 87 sampled), which alone moves the Rogan-Gladen estimate by about +19,000. The only estimators that came within a factor of 1.5 of the true 552 (PPV/FOM transport, ratio, calibrated encoder probability sums, a gate plus last year's miss rate: 510-640) work because the pooled rare share hardly changed (7.8 per 10,000 in 2025, 8.3 in 2026). Copying last year's rate, with no coder at all, gives 518 (-6%), and in PPV/FOM about two-thirds of the estimate is last year's miss rate. Family counts behave the same way. No coder-based estimator beats last year's counts on summed error (best 166 vs 168 at level 1), Rogan-Gladen and the matrix method (BBSE) blow up, and EM on the encoder probabilities diverges (to 140,000 or to 0). Growth rankings agree only weakly with true growth (Spearman 0.1-0.55, nothing picked in advance stands out). Counting is not hopeless everywhere. For codes that are not attractors, raw LLM output counts do follow real shifts: Computer System Security rose from 16 to 88 reports, and the Opus and Gemma zero-shot answers in that group rose about 5x, with no sampled false answers in either year. But two of the three named new habits cannot be seen from the coders' outputs. Power Conditioning Problem rose from 5 to 34 and no coder ever names it; Medication Error actually fell from 156 to 78, and the coders read those reports as flow problems. The question also needs reframing: MAUDE already gives a filed code on every report, so counting filed codes is a database query. An estimate from the coders only matters where codes are missing or untrusted, and there a same-year audit of about 18,000 uniformly drawn labelled reports (about 41,000 for ±33%) does the job without any coder. Gating by a coder's flags only cuts that to about 11,000-13,000.

findings.claim: The loader passes the sanity check, and the 2026 year is rebuilt exactly.
findings.evidence: Encoder 2026: 32 right / 166 false (1 sampled), uniform accuracy 0.6365; 2025: 60 / 1, 0.7482. Zero-shot 2026: Qwen 131 / 14,693 (88), Gemma 158 / 14,476 (87), Opus 154 / 6,665 (40); retrieval 79 / 2,734, 92 / 2,235, 95 / 3,026. The weighted pseudo-population sums to 661,160 reports in 2026 (3,956 balanced + 657,204 natural) and 762,360 in 2025, with 552 and 597 rare reports (balanced and natural parts do not overlap).

findings.claim: How I set up the problem. The 2026 raw output count is treated as known, as if the coder had been run on the whole year, so the 2026 test-side sampling error is set to zero. The intervals resample only the 2025 development year (stratified bootstrap over rare census, balanced non-rare, 6-20 stratum and uniform rows). My own evaluation is still noisy: the 2026 raw count comes from the uniform draw, with an SD of about 1,000 for Opus zero-shot and about 5 for the strict rules.
findings.evidence: eval_sd_raw2026 in s3_pooled.json: Opus zs 1,032, Opus rag 682, Opus cor 326, enc 159, enc_and_zs 5.

findings.claim: Pooled 2026 estimates (truth 552): raw counts and Rogan-Gladen (the standard 2x2 correction for 'rare vs not') are useless. The strict rules give tight but biased answers, because their recall drifts.
findings.evidence: Rogan-Gladen [95% interval from 2025 noise only]: Opus zs 3,400 [-3,068, 9,555]; Opus rag 7,294 [845, 13,117]; Gemma zs 20,026 [11,531, 28,909]; Qwen zs 6,652 [-1,214, 14,971]; encoder 1,938 [1,556, 2,515] (x3.5); Opus prior-corrected 818 [-5,274, 5,636]; enc_and_zs (Opus) 387 [292, 573] (x0.70); Qwen prior-corrected 430 [317, 613] (x0.78). Raw counts: Opus zs 6,819 (x12), encoder 198 (x0.36), Qwen prior-corrected 30.

findings.claim: The estimators that land near 552 do so by carrying over last year's base rate, not by reading the coders.
findings.evidence: Last year's rate, no coder (597 x 661,160 / 762,360): 518 (-6%). PPV/FOM transport (count = flagged x 2025 precision + unflagged x 2025 miss rate): Opus zs 540 [497, 617], Qwen zs 547 [511, 605], Gemma zs 606 [557, 688], encoder 663 [650, 675]. For Opus zs, the flagged part is about 6,819 x 0.027 = 184; the remaining ~356 is 654,000 unflagged x 5.5 per 10,000 (2025 miss rate). Ratio estimator (raw26 x truth25 / raw25): Opus zs 592 [446, 851], Gemma zs 828 [660, 1,108]. The true pooled rate went from 7.83 to 8.35 per 10,000.

findings.claim: Prior estimation from the encoder's stored probabilities fails without a calibration step. EM diverges, and the plain probability sum overestimates by about 1.5x in both years.
findings.evidence: Probability sum (PCC): 2025 879 vs truth 597; 2026 943 vs 552 (evaluation SD 60). EM (Saerens) with the training-frequency source prior: 171,432 (2025) and 139,975 (2026); with a uniform source prior it collapses to 0. PCC was the variant chosen on 2025; PCC calibrated by the 2025 ratio gives 640 (x1.16). The encoder's own year-on-year change (+7%) points the wrong way (truth -8%).
findings.reproduce: s5_em.py -> s5_em.out (the 'rho(own change)' lines for *_calibrated variants are wrong: they divide by the uncalibrated 2025 value; ignore them)

findings.claim: The two rates the 2x2 adjustment needs are not stable from 2025 to 2026. Even shifts too small to detect move the estimate by several times the truth.
findings.evidence: Rate of naming a rare code on rare reports (recall), 2025 -> 2026: Opus zs 0.307 -> 0.355; Opus rag 0.181 -> 0.254; encoder 0.102 -> 0.062; enc_and_zs 0.062 -> 0.043; Qwen prior-corrected 0.064 -> 0.053. False-alarm rate into rare codes per 10,000 ordinary reports [uniform sampled]: Opus zs 87.8 [35] -> 100.3 [40]; Gemma zs 136.2 [54] -> 218.8 [87] (2024val: 140.0, 140/9,997); Qwen zs 190.1 [75] -> 221.5 [88] (2024val 205.1); Qwen rag 22.9 [9] -> 40.6 [16]; Gemma rag 33.0 [13] -> 33.3 [13]; Opus prior-corrected 10.0 [4] -> 10.2 [4]; encoder 0 [0] -> 2.5 [1]. Moving from the 2025 false-alarm rate to the 2026 one shifts the Rogan-Gladen estimate by: Opus zs +2,760, Opus rag +6,522, Gemma zs +19,432, Qwen zs +6,117, Gemma rag +101. The recall drift alone moves the strict rules by +96 to +219 (17-40% of the truth).

findings.claim: Labels needed. Measuring the false-alarm rate in a past year cannot get a cross-year pooled count within x1.5. A same-year audit needs about 18,000-41,000 labels, and a coder gate cuts that by only 20-40%.
findings.evidence: Allowed error in the false-alarm rate for a 95% half-width of T/3 (184): 0.4-0.9 per 10,000. Labelled uniform reports needed: Opus zs 4.9 M, Gemma zs 8.4 M, Qwen zs 8.0 M, rag rules 3-5 M, Opus prior-corrected 3.3 M, Qwen prior-corrected 48,220. Same-year uniform audit: 18,390 labels (±T/2) or 41,377 (±T/3). Stratified audit, Neyman allocation, by gate (share of year flagged; rare recall): Opus zs flag (1.03%; 0.355) 13,560 / 30,510; any of the 7 answers rare (3.61%; 0.473) 13,069 / 29,406; encoder rare-mass >= 0.00352 (7.07%; 0.553) 13,040 / 29,340; union (9.89%; 0.672) 11,797 / 26,544; mass >= 0.000352 (34.5%; 0.935) 11,029 / 24,815. Labelling the whole gate plus a sample outside: e.g. 46,747 + 7,650. Gated census plus last year's miss rate outside the gate: 567 (encoder-mass gate) and 579 (gate at 1/10 of the threshold) vs 552. This works only because the miss rate stayed put (4.26 -> 4.02 per 10,000).

findings.claim: Family counts (16 IMDRF level-1 families, 34 level-2 groups of the rare codes): no coder-based estimator beats copying last year's counts.
findings.evidence: Level 1, sum of absolute errors over families (median abs. error): last year's counts 168 (6.5); best PPV/FOM: Gemma prior-corrected 166 (6.8), Qwen prior-corrected 170, Gemma zs 190 (7.6), Opus zs 475; ratio estimator 519-13,426; Rogan-Gladen and BBSE thousands to billions (unstable). Level 2: last year 363 (4.3); PPV/FOM 324-1,654. Share of families within x1.5: last year 0.44 (L1), PPV/FOM 0.31-0.56. True changes the carry-over cannot see: Computer System Security group 16 -> 88, Electrical Power 6 -> 36, Implant subsidence 109 -> 63, Application Program 159 -> 79, Protective Measures 16 -> 2.

findings.claim: Trend detection is weak overall. Rank correlation of estimated with true growth sits between about 0.1 and 0.55, and none of the coder-estimator pairs could have been picked in advance as the good one.
findings.evidence: L1 Spearman of raw-output growth vs true growth: -0.22 to 0.37 across coders; estimator growth up to 0.55 (Opus prior-corrected raw). Per code (46), raw output growth: Opus zs 0.30. Restricted to codes with no sampled uniform false answer in 2025 (screen set on 2025): Opus zs 0.50 (n=32), flags 'rose >=2x and by >=5' 3 right, 2 false, 3 missed; Opus prior-corrected 0.45 (n=42); Gemma zs 0.31; encoder 0.15. With 16-46 units, the SE of Spearman is about 0.15-0.26, and I compared many coder/estimator pairs, so the best values are partly selection.

findings.claim: The named new habits, case by case. Computer System Security shows up in aggregate LLM outputs. Power Conditioning Problem is never named by any coder. 'Medication Error' did not rise: it fell, and its 2026 reports read as flow problems.
findings.evidence: Computer System Security Problem, truth 14 -> 67 (group 16 -> 88): Opus zs names it 4 -> 20 times on rare reports (all right), plus 'Application Security Problem' 7 -> 44; Gemma zs 4 -> 37; 0 sampled uniform false answers in both years. Power Conditioning Problem, 5 -> 34: 0 outputs from any coder in either year; Opus zs says 'Power Problem' on 20 of its 34 reports. Application Program Problem: Medication Error, 156 -> 78: Opus zs names it 9 -> 0 times on these reports and answers 'Excess Flow or Over-Infusion' on 24 of 78; its false answers elsewhere are 393 -> 499 a year (2 -> 3 sampled). Extra Components 10 -> 28: Opus zs right 8 -> 20. Biofilm 2 -> 18: Opus zs 0 -> 9. Encoder probability mass for these codes barely moves (Power Conditioning 16.7 -> 18.2, Security 28.6 -> 38.4, mostly on non-rare reports).

findings.claim: What can be tested honestly on the current data. The rare census contains every rare report, so a coder's output count on those rows is the exact full-year number. False answers on ordinary reports are known only from the ~4,000-report uniform draw. So 'the output count for code X rose' is solid only where the false part is small, and 0 sampled false still allows roughly 500 a year per code. A real test needs coder outputs on all reports of both years.
findings.evidence: Compute for full-year runs, from round 1 (arithmetic s3_cost): Qwen zs about 113 GPU-hours per year, Gemma zs 179, Opus zs about 7.7 B cache-read tokens per year; both years needed. The encoder on the full year would need a GPU too (RoBERTa-large on 661k reports is impractical on CPU).

findings.claim: The question needs reframing. In MAUDE every report carries the filed code, so 'how many rare-code reports were filed' is a database query, and any estimator here is benchmarked against a number that is free. A count from the coders helps only where codes are missing, untrusted, or absent (another corpus); there the realistic tool is a same-year labelled audit, not a corrected count.
findings.evidence: pool_codes_2026.json gives the exact count per code (rare total 552); estimators above can at best reproduce it.

leads: Alerting instead of counting (needs GPU, about 113-180 GPU-h per LLM per year, user approval): run Qwen or Gemma zero-shot on all reports of 2025 and 2026 and flag codes whose output count jumps, limited to non-attractor codes (screen set on earlier years). This is the only signal that tracked a real new habit (Computer System Security). Test on 2024 -> 2025 first.

Same-year audit design (CPU plus human labels): if a count is needed where codes are untrusted, draw about 13,000 labels stratified by the encoder rare-mass union gate. That gives ±50% on the pooled count; no coder correction needed.

Novelty detection without labels (CPU only): count new near-duplicate text templates (e.g. first 200 characters, hashed) that appear in 2026 and not in 2025 across the whole pool. Check whether the Power Conditioning, Medication Error and Security reports fall into new templates, and how many new templates appear overall (the false-alert rate). The pools are already cached in wf1/convention and wf1/ceiling.

Watch for code-sibling drift: on 2026 Security reports the LLMs name the child 'Application Security Problem' about as often as the parent. Group-level counting absorbs this (CPU; already in s7/s8 data).
Do not pursue Rogan-Gladen, BBSE or EM at this prevalence. Their failure is structural (they need the false-alarm rate known to about 1 in 100,000 and stable across years), not a tuning problem.
caveats: The 2026 'full-year' raw counts are themselves estimates from the weighted samples. My errors for the loose coders carry evaluation noise of about ±1,000 (Opus zs SD 1,032), which does not change the verdict, since their Rogan-Gladen errors are thousands to tens of thousands.
The bootstrap intervals cover only 2025 sampling noise, not year-to-year drift. That is why they often miss the truth: at family level, 19-88% of intervals cover it.
The EM evaluation spread used only 15 resamples, after the first run with 100 resamples ran over 20 minutes and I stopped it. The EM bootstrap is coarse.
For calibrated variants, the 'own change' Spearman lines in s5_em.out use the wrong denominator (a bug). Ignore them; the uncalibrated PCC line gives the encoder's own change.

Rules with code screens from round 1 were left out of the pooled analysis: their screens are built on 2025 false answers, so their 2025 false-alarm rate would be biased low by construction. I used an unscreened version (encoder base + zs_and_rag + encoder confidence < 0.5) instead.

The pooled 'within x1.5' result for PPV/FOM, ratio and gate+miss-rate estimators depends on the rare share being stable between these two years (+7%). One pair of years cannot show how often that holds.
Rank correlations rest on 16-46 units, with many coder/estimator pairs compared; the best values are partly selection, not chosen in advance.

No GPU, no API calls, and no human reading was used. Another investigator's Python process ran at the same time as mine for a while; I ran only one at a time myself and stopped my own stray EM process.
surprises: The false-alarm rate into rare codes is not a stable property of a coder. Gemma zero-shot sat at 140 per 10,000 in 2024val and 136 in 2025, then jumped to 219 in 2026 (54 -> 87 sampled). Opus retrieval and Qwen retrieval rose by 1.6-1.8x.
'Medication Error', cited in round 1 as a new 2026 habit, fell from 156 to 78 reports. What changed is how the reports read: the LLMs call them flow problems.

The encoder's summed probability for rare codes over-predicts the rare share by a near-constant factor (1.47 in 2025, 1.71 in 2026). The year-to-year change in that sum points the wrong way (+7% vs truth -8%).

Sibling confusion helps group counts: on 2026 Computer System Security reports the LLMs mostly answer the child 'Application Security Problem', so the group-level output count (~5x rise) follows the true group rise (16 -> 88) better than any single code does.

checks.claim: Loader sanity: 2026 encoder 32/166 (1), accuracy 0.6365; 2025 60/1, 0.7482; zero-shot and retrieval counts for all three LLMs; the 2026 pseudo-population sums to 661,160 with 552 rare reports, and 2025 to 762,360 with 597.
checks.detail: Measured with my own loader (c1_load.py, rare_limits.load_year + score). Every number matches: enc 32/166(1) 0.6365, 2025 60/1(0) 0.7482; zs Qwen 131/14,693(88), Gemma 158/14,476(87), Opus 154/6,665(40); rag 79/2,734(16), 92/2,235(13), 95/3,026(18); prior-corrected Opus 58/707(4), Qwen 27/3(0). N26 661,160, T26 552, N25 762,360, T25 597 (c2_pooled.py).

checks.claim: Rogan-Gladen from 2025 rates blows up: Opus zs 3,400, Opus rag 7,294, Gemma zs 20,026, Qwen zs 6,652, encoder 1,938, Opus prior-corrected 818, enc_and_zs 387, Qwen prior-corrected 430.
checks.detail: Measured, my code: Opus zs 3,400, Opus rag 7,294, Gemma zs 20,026, Qwen zs 6,652, encoder 1,938, Opus cor 818, Opus enc_and_zs 387, Qwen cor 430. If I put the 2026 false-alarm rate in instead of the 2025 one, Rogan-Gladen lands at 540-780 for the zs and rag coders. So the blow-up comes from transporting the false-alarm rate between years, not from the formula itself. I did not re-run the bootstrap intervals.

checks.claim: Headline: a pooled count needs the false-alarm rate known to about 1 in 100,000, and measuring it would take 3-8 million labelled ordinary reports.
checks.detail: Measured: the allowed 95% half-width of the false-alarm rate for +-T/3 is 8.3 (Opus zs), 7.8 (Gemma zs), 9.5 (Qwen zs), 5.0-5.5 (rag), 3.4 (Opus cor) and 1.7-2.8 (strict rules) per 100,000. Their body says 0.4-0.9 per 10,000, which matches. For the zero-shot coders the headline's '1 in 100,000' is about 8x too strict. The label arithmetic (1.96^2 f / allow^2) reproduces about 4.9 M for Opus zs. But 3-8 M is only the cost of estimating the rate from a uniform sample. The false part of a coder's flags can be counted exactly in the same year by labelling every flagged report (about 6,800 for Opus zs, about 14,800 for Qwen or Gemma zs). That is the 'all-gated' design they compute themselves. What binds is year-to-year drift plus the miss part outside the flags, not the cost of measuring the rate (inferred).

checks.claim: The false-alarm rate shifts between years by more than the allowance; Gemma zs went from 136 to 219 per 10,000 (54 vs 87 sampled), which alone moves Rogan-Gladen by about +19,000.
checks.detail: Measured: Gemma zs 136.2 [54/3,985] -> 218.8 [87/3,974] per 10,000. The binomial test on the sampled counts gives p = 0.005, so this shift is real. The Rogan-Gladen move is +19,414. With about 30 per 10,000 SE on the rate difference, its rough 95% range is +6,000 to +33,000 (inferred). The other shifts are not distinguishable from sampling noise: Opus zs 35 -> 40 (p = 0.57), Qwen zs 75 -> 88 (p = 0.31), Opus rag 11 -> 18 (p = 0.20), Qwen rag 9 -> 16 (p = 0.17). So the surprise that 'Opus and Qwen retrieval rose 1.6-1.8x' is not established. The accurate statement is weaker but still decisive: one uniform year measures the rate only to about +-15-30 per 10,000. That is 20-40x coarser than the allowance, so no one can tell whether the rate is stable to the needed level.

checks.claim: Estimators near 552 just carry over last year's base rate: persistence 518 (-6%); PPV/FOM Opus zs 540 (about two-thirds is last year's miss rate), Qwen zs 547, Gemma zs 606, encoder 663; ratio Opus zs 592, Gemma 828; pooled rate 7.83 -> 8.35 per 10,000.
checks.detail: Measured: persistence 517.8; rate 7.83 -> 8.35 per 10,000. PPV/FOM Opus zs 540 = 182 from the flags + 359 from the 2025 miss rate on the unflagged reports (66%). Qwen zs 547 (331 of it from the miss rate), Gemma zs 606, encoder 663, Opus cor 521, Gemma cor 514. Ratio Opus zs 592, Gemma zs 828. The interpretation holds: every PPV/FOM estimate sits between 508 and 663 whatever the coder, which is the signature of a carried-over prior. It survives sampling: the miss part depends on the 552/597 census counts, not on the uniform draw.

checks.claim: Encoder probability sum (PCC) overestimates about 1.5x (2025: 879 vs 597; 2026: 943 vs 552); calibrated PCC gives 640; EM diverges (140,000 or 0).
checks.detail: Measured PCC: 879 vs 597 and 943 vs 552 (the 2026 PCC/truth ratio is 1.71, not 1.5). Calibrated 943 x 597/879 = 640 (arithmetic). I did not re-run EM. Their code divides by training-frequency priors as the source prior. The encoder is class-balanced, so its outputs do not carry training frequencies, and that variant is misspecified by construction. Its blow-up to 140k shows the misspecification more than a property of EM. The uniform-prior variant collapsing to 0 still fails. The conclusion 'EM is not usable here' stands, but the stated reason is not shown.

checks.claim: Same-year audit: 18,390 uniform labels for +-T/2 and 41,377 for +-T/3; a gate (Neyman) cuts it to about 11,000-13,000 (+-T/2); gated census + 2025 outside rate gives 567 and 579.
checks.detail: Measured: 18,390 and 41,377. The gate threshold is 0.00352, set as the 95th percentile of 2025 uniform non-rare rows, so it was chosen on 2025. Gate share 7.07%, recall 0.5525, Neyman 13,040 (+-T/2) and 29,340 (+-T/3); thr/10: 11,029 and 24,815. Hindsight check: allocating with 2025 in/out prevalences gives 13,042 and 11,206, so the allocation is not sensitive to the 2026 truth. Gate + transported miss rate: 305 + 614,413 x 4.26e-4 = 567; 516 + 432,884 x 1.45e-4 = 579. The 2026 outside rate is 4.02e-4. Caveat (inferred): applying a gate to a real year needs the encoder run on every report, which was not done. Here the gate flags exist only for sampled rows (276 uniform rows flagged).

checks.claim: Headline: a same-year audit of about 18,000 uniform labelled reports 'does the job'.
checks.detail: 18,390 gives a 95% half-width of T/2, i.e. 276 to 828. That is a factor-2 band, not the x1.5 standard the rest of the report uses. For roughly x1.5 the figure is 41,377 (Neyman with a gate: 25,000-29,000). The comparison with 3-8 M also mixes targets (T/2 against T/3), though the gap is large enough that the conclusion holds.

checks.claim: Family counts (16 level-1 families): no coder-based estimator beats last year's counts (best 166 vs 168).
checks.detail: Measured: persistence summed abs error 168; PPV/FOM Gemma prior-corrected 166, Qwen prior-corrected 170, Opus zs 475. 166 < 168, so strictly one estimator does beat the carry-over, by 2 reports. The fair statement is 'none does meaningfully better'. Family truths reproduced (e.g. Patient Device Interaction 109 -> 63, Protective Measures 16 -> 2, Manufacturing 10 -> 28). BBSE and the level-2 numbers were not re-checked.

checks.claim: Trend detection is weak: per-code Spearman of Opus zs raw growth vs true growth 0.30; others 0.1-0.55.
checks.detail: Measured, my own definition (log of (x+1) ratios, 46 rare codes, whole-year weighted counts): 0.305. Other pairs were not re-checked. With n = 16-46 and many pairs compared, values up to 0.55 are consistent with selection, as they say.

checks.claim: Computer System Security: truth 14 -> 67 (group 16 -> 88); Opus and Gemma zero-shot answers in that group rose about 5x, with no sampled false answers in either year.
checks.detail: Measured truth: 14 -> 67, and Application Security 2 -> 21 (group 16 -> 88). Opus zs on the parent code: right 4 -> 20, false 0 -> 6, 0 sampled. But Opus zs names the child 'Application Security Problem' about 375 times a year in 2026 (5 right, 370 false), and 2 of those false answers are in the uniform draw (my run; their own s7 output shows '331 other [2u]'). So 'no sampled false answers' is wrong for Opus at the group level. Opus's whole-year group output goes 17 -> 401 (about 24x) against a true 5.5x. The 'about 5x' holds only on the rare-census rows (11 -> 64), which a real pipeline cannot separate out. Gemma zs: group 4 -> 54 whole-year (about 13x), 0 sampled false. So Gemma tracks the direction with no sampled false, but overshoots the size. Coarse: 2 sampled rows = 328 a year, and 0 sampled still allows several hundred.
