checks.claim: Power Conditioning Problem rose 5 -> 34 and no coder ever names it; Medication Error fell 156 -> 78 and the coders read those reports as flow problems.
checks.detail: Measured: Power Conditioning truth 5 -> 34, and 0 outputs from enc, zs or rag of any LLM in either year. It is not one of the 47 held-out codes (it is in the 424-label list), so the miss is not a list artifact. Opus zs answers 'Power Problem' on 20 of the 34. Medication Error 156 -> 78; per report 2.05 -> 1.18 per 10,000, so the fall holds even though 2026 covers only 10 months. Opus zs right 9 -> 0, false 393 -> 499 (2 -> 3 sampled), 'Excess Flow or Over-Infusion' on 24 of 78 (in 2025: 'Application Program Problem' 25 of 156). Siblings in the same family moved a lot too (e.g. parent Electrical Power Problem 200 -> 10, Loss of Power 10 -> 174), but these rest on 0-1 sampled uniform rows each and are too coarse to read.

checks.claim: A real test needs full-year coder runs (Qwen zs about 113 GPU-h, Gemma about 179 per year).
checks.detail: Compute figures come from round 1 and I did not re-derive them. The logic (the uniform draw cannot resolve per-code false counts below about 500 a year) is consistent with 0 sampled allowing about 3.7 x 164 = 600 a year (inferred).

corrections: Headline '1 in 100,000' is too strict: for the zero-shot coders the allowed 95% error in the false-alarm rate is 7.8-9.5 per 100,000; strict rules 1.7-3.4 per 100,000.

'3-8 million labels to measure the rate' applies only to estimating it from a uniform sample. Labelling every flagged report (about 6,800 for Opus zs, about 14,800 for Qwen or Gemma zs) gives the same-year false count exactly. The real blockers are year-to-year drift and the miss part outside the flags.

Only the Gemma zs false-alarm shift (54 -> 87 sampled, p = 0.005) is established. Opus zs (35 -> 40), Qwen zs (75 -> 88), Opus rag (11 -> 18) and Qwen rag (9 -> 16) are within sampling noise. Drop the surprise 'Opus and Qwen retrieval rose 1.6-1.8x' or mark it unestablished. The +19,000 Gemma move has a rough 95% range of +6,000 to +33,000.
'18,000 uniform labels does the job' is for +-50% (a factor-2 band). The x1.5 standard used elsewhere needs about 41,000 uniform, or 25,000-29,000 with a gate.
Family level: Gemma prior-corrected PPV/FOM (166) beats persistence (168) by 2. Say 'no estimator does meaningfully better', not 'none beats'.

Computer System Security: Opus zs has 2 sampled uniform false answers in 2026 (on the child Application Security Problem, about 330 a year). Its whole-year group output rises about 24x (17 -> 401), not 5x. The 5x holds only on the rare-census rows. Gemma's whole-year group output rises about 13x with 0 sampled false. So 'raw output counts follow real shifts' is direction-only, and only for Gemma here.

EM: the train-frequency source prior is misspecified for a class-balanced encoder, so the 140,000 blow-up says little about EM itself. PCC overestimates 1.47x (2025) and 1.71x (2026), not 'about 1.5x in both years'.
check.net: Every core number reproduces from my own loader, including the sanity check, Rogan-Gladen, PPV/FOM, persistence 518, PCC, the audit sizes and the gate. The main conclusion stands: the coder-based pooled estimates that come near 552 do so by carrying over last year's miss rate (two-thirds of Opus's PPV/FOM is the 2025 miss rate). Rogan-Gladen fails as soon as the false-alarm rate is moved from one year to the next, and a same-year labelled audit of tens of thousands of reports beats any correction. The headline overstates three supports. The precision requirement is about 8 per 100,000, not 1. The 3-8 M label cost applies only to one inefficient design (labelling the flags measures the false part exactly). Only Gemma's year-to-year rate shift is statistically real, though one year of uniform data cannot show stability at the needed level either. The 'counting tracks new habits' example is weaker than stated: Opus has sampled false answers in the Security group and overshoots about 24x, and Gemma's direction is right but about 13x against a true 5.5x. The Power Conditioning and Medication Error findings hold, and Power Conditioning is in the label list, so its miss is not caused by the list.

pilots.title: Last year's mistakes and filings as memory: do they remove false rare answers without killing right ones?

report.headline: A memory of earlier filings removes the template-driven part of the false rare answers, but not most of them. Its largest effect is on Opus. The filing-memory veto was planned in advance and its settings were fixed on 2025. It drops a rare proposal when the nearest earlier reports were nearly all filed under one frequent code. On 2026 it takes Opus zero-shot from 154 right / 6,665 false a year (40 sampled false) to 143 / 2,874 (17). Qwen goes from 131 / 14,693 (88) to 123 / 9,052 (54) and Gemma from 158 / 14,476 (87) to 149 / 8,690 (52). So about 40-57% of false answers go and about 6-8% of right answers are lost. The memory needs to be fresh: 2025 filings alone do as well as 2024+2025, and 2024 filings alone do much worse. For Opus, 20 of the 23 sampled false answers the veto removes are the two known manufacturer templates (Battery High Impedance 10, Failure to Reset 10). What is left is a scatter of one-off near misses, often the rare child of a filed parent code. A memory of last year's audited mistakes, keyed by (rare code, encoder code), works well on Opus: 154 / 2,390 (14) with no right answer lost. That key is a hindsight choice: the planned tuning could not test it, because the 2024 validation set has no right rare answers to guard with. The planned choice (TF-IDF similarity to a remembered false text) removes only 7-17% of false answers. Adding 'zero-shot and retrieval agree' to the veto gives Opus 76 / 869 (5), but round 1's best simple rule already reached 94 / 873 (5). No version gets false at or below right, so memory alone does not solve the problem. The earlier Opus second look failed for three main reasons. The alternative code it offered was rarely the filed code (17 of 63 false proposals on 2026nat). In 34 of 63 the filed code was the parent of the proposed rare code. And Opus kept the literal rare code even when the frequent code's examples were the same template (28 of 32).

findings.claim: The loader reproduces the known encoder numbers.
findings.evidence: Encoder 2026: 32 right / 166 false a year (1 sampled), uniform-draw accuracy 0.6365. Encoder 2025: 60 / 1 (0 sampled), accuracy 0.7482. Identical for all three LLM loads. Zero-shot baselines also match: Qwen 131/14,693.4 (88), Gemma 158/14,476 (87), Opus 154/6,664.7 (40); retrieval 79/2,733.5 (16), 92/2,235.2 (13), 95/3,025.6 (18).

findings.claim: B, the planned test: the filing-memory veto (t=0.4, m=2, s=0.6, chosen on 2025 with the 2024 pool as memory) cuts false rare answers by about 40-57% at a cost of about 6-8% of right ones. With 2024+2025 as memory it was applied once to 2026.
Fresher memory, not bigger memory, is what helps. 2025 filings alone match 2024+2025; 2024 filings alone are much weaker on 2026.
findings.evidence: Opus zs false a year with memory 2024 / 2025 / both: 4,844 (29) / 2,873 (17) / 2,874 (17). Qwen zs: 11,027 (66) / 9,061 (54) / 9,052 (54). Gemma zs: 11,489 (69) / 8,856 (53) / 8,690 (52). Right answers stay within 123-152. The stored 10 training-set neighbours (nb_vote share >= 0.7, chosen on 2025) give Opus zs 120/2,352 (14), Qwen 108/6,538 (39), Gemma 119/7,035 (42): about as few false answers but 9-34 more right answers lost.

findings.claim: For Opus, the veto works almost entirely on the two known manufacturer templates.
findings.evidence: Opus zs uniform-draw false answers on 2026, dropped by the veto: Battery Problem: High Impedance 10 of 10, Failure to Reset 10 of 15, and 3 others. The 17 kept are spread over about 10 codes with 1-5 each: Failure to Reset 5, Decoupling 2, Precipitate 2, Medication Error 2, Prophylactic removal 2, and others with 1.

findings.claim: A, the planned choice: the error-memory key picked by the pre-stated rule (2024val -> 2025, Qwen and Gemma) was TF-IDF similarity to any remembered false text at >= 0.6. It removes few false answers.
findings.evidence: 2026 zs: Qwen 131/13,372 (80), Gemma 158/13,319 (80), Opus 154/5,515 (33). Rag: Qwen and Gemma unchanged, Opus 95/1,875 (11). No right answer is lost. The exact template key (first 200 normalised characters) never matched across years: 0 of the 2026 false answers.

findings.claim: A, a hindsight choice: the key (rare code, encoder code), with the guard 'not right in 2025 balanced + census', is the strongest single memory result for Opus. It was not chosen by the planned tuning.
findings.evidence: Opus zs 2026: 154/2,390 (14), base 154/6,665 (40). 29 of 40 sampled false answers had a seen key; 47 of 154 right answers did too, but all 47 were protected by the guard. Opus rag: 95/1,382 (8). Qwen zs: 121/8,579 (51). Gemma zs: 155/6,232 (37). (code, neighbour-vote code): Gemma zs 151/4,733 (28), Qwen zs 120/7,721 (46), Opus zs 153/2,390 (14). The planned tuning could not see these keys because 2024val has 0 right rare answers for Qwen and Gemma. With nothing to protect right answers there, the code-level keys deleted most of them (Qwen zs 2025: 58 of 201 kept with code+enc).

findings.claim: Veto and error memory together, plus agreement of zero-shot and retrieval, give the cleanest pairs. They still do not beat round 1's best simple Opus rule.
findings.evidence: 2026: veto + code+enc (hindsight) gives Opus zs 143/2,048 (12), Qwen zs 113/6,732 (40), Gemma zs 146/5,219 (31). Veto + zs==rag gives Opus 76/869 (5), Qwen 65/1,062 (6), Gemma 78/1,701 (10). Round 1's best Opus rule: 94/873 (5).

findings.evidence: Add rule (chosen on 2025: place a rare code when >= 1 of the top-10 neighbours at cosine >= 0.4 carries it): 2026 gives 14 right / 686 false (4) with 2024+2025 memory, 14/524 (3) with 2025 only, 5/164 (1) with 2024 only. On 2025 it gave 22/3 (0).

findings.claim: The Opus second look barely separated right from false proposals.
findings.evidence: 2026nat, 121 checks: right proposals kept 41/58 (71%), false proposals kept 50/63 (79%). 2026 balanced: right 38/52, false 24/34.

findings.claim: The second look usually offered the wrong alternative code. The most common false case was the rare child of a filed parent code.
findings.evidence: 2026nat false proposals (63): filed code = the offered alternative in 17 (Opus still kept the rare code 12 times); filed code = parent/ancestor of the rare code in 34 (kept rare 30); other family 10; sibling 1; same top family 1. Example: proposed Application Security Problem, filed Computer System Security Problem, alternative offered Computer Software Problem.

findings.claim: Opus judged by the literal meaning of the report, not by how this kind of report is filed, even when the frequent code's examples were the same template.
findings.evidence: 2026nat false proposals where the report's first 6 words equal those of a shown example of the frequent code: Opus kept the rare code 28 of 32. Reading example 24135756: the report is the 'code 1003' CRT-P template, and all 5 shown Premature Discharge examples begin with the same template. Opus still chose High Impedance because the report says 'potential high impedance within the battery'. The examples were clipped at 300 characters, before the analysis sentence, so they could not show that this exact wording is filed as Premature Discharge. On right proposals dropped (7 of the 10 read are Implant subsidence vs Migration), Opus sometimes switched to wording similarity instead, saying it 'chose code 2 because the report matches its examples closely in wording'.

findings.claim: The stored second-look parser misreads some answers that include an explanation.
findings.evidence: 68 of 379 answers were longer than a digit. Taking the first digit instead of the last changes 29 of 379 verdicts (15 of 121 on 2026nat). Read example: answer '**1** ... code 2 does not fit' was parsed as 2. Re-parsing does not rescue separation: 2026nat right kept 43/58, false kept 55/63.

findings.claim: A check that could work would have to show the filing history of the report's own wording, as counts, and include the filed parent and siblings among the choices. The veto already does the first part mechanically, so an LLM check on top would add little.
findings.evidence: Based on the C findings above plus B: the veto removes exactly the template families that the second look kept.

leads: Stack the filing-memory veto (t=0.4, m=2, s=0.6, memory = all earlier filings) on round 1's best Opus rule (94/873, 5 sampled) and on the encoder-gate rule. Needs only CPU and the existing knn_*.npz files; the rule outputs must be regenerated from rare_limits.accept.

Make the memory rolling within 2026: add earlier 2026 months to the memory using the report dates (wf1/convention/cache_dates2026.pkl). This needs a dated kNN, about 20 minutes of CPU. The freshness result suggests it should help most.

Re-tune error-memory keys properly. Use the 2025 balanced set + census as the guard for a 2025-half -> 2025-other-half split (cross-fitting by report). That gives a non-hindsight test of the (code, encoder code) key on 2026 for all three LLMs. CPU only.

Change the target: score 'rare code or its filed parent' as a hierarchy-aware review flag. 34 of 63 false second-look cases were child-vs-filed-parent. Needs a human decision on whether such near misses count as errors.

Redesign the second look (needs API credit or local Qwen/Gemma on GPU, with the owner's go-ahead). Show the counts of how the report's nearest earlier wording was filed, use full-length examples (no 300-char clip), offer the parent, the siblings and the memory's majority code as alternatives, and parse the first digit (or force a single token).

Get a bigger uniform draw. The best pairs rest on 4-17 sampled false answers. About 600 a year is the floor the current draw cannot resolve. Needs LLM outputs on more uniform reports (local GPU or API).
surprises: The 2024 filing memory has gone stale by 2026. With the same rule, the 2024 pool removes far fewer 2026 false answers than the 2025 pool alone (Opus zs 4,844 vs 2,873 a year), while on 2025 the 2024 pool worked well. Filing habits drift from year to year.

The 2024 validation set (10,000 training-year reports) contains no right rare answers from Qwen or Gemma, so 'last year's right answers' cannot guard anything in the planned tuning. This makes code-level error keys look ruinous in tuning and strong on 2026.
Exact first-200-character templates of 2025 false answers never recur among 2026 false answers (0 matches). The templates recur only loosely: same family, different numbers and dates.
Over half of the second look's false proposals (34 of 63 on 2026nat) were the rare child of the filed parent code. These are near misses, not wild errors.

When the frequent code's examples were the same manufacturer template as the report, Opus still kept the literal rare code 28 of 32 times. The 300-character clip removed the very sentence ('high impedance within the battery') that showed the template is filed as Premature Discharge.
The stored second-look parser took the last '1'/'2' anywhere in the answer. In 29 of 379 answers this differs from the first digit, and at least one read case was misparsed.
caveats: All 2026 false counts rest on small sampled counts (4-54 sampled; one sampled report is about 164 a year). The 'best' pairs (5, 12, 14 sampled) have Poisson spreads of roughly +-50-90%.

The (code, encoder code) and (code, neighbour-vote code) error keys, the zs==rag combination with the veto, and the combined rows in s8 were chosen after seeing 2026. They are hindsight. Only the veto (t=0.4, m=2, s=0.6) and the TF-IDF@0.6 error key were fixed before 2026. The zs==rag + veto pair was checked to behave the same on 2025.

Counts are for each LLM arm's rare answers alone (dropped answers count as not placed). This is not a full coding system. Whatever replaces a dropped answer, for example the encoder's own rare answers (32/166), is not added.

Part B's TF-IDF uses the first 1,500 lowercased characters, hashing to 2^20 features, word 1-2 grams, sublinear tf, and idf fitted on the 2024 pool only. The 63 rows of the 2025 pool whose code is outside the label list count as unknown neighbours.
In my coder cache, text_len is wrong (load_items was patched with texts cut at 1,500 characters). It is not used anywhere in these analyses; selector picks were not recomputed.
Part C used Opus's stored verdicts. I read 20 false-kept and 10 right-dropped cases myself. No human read anything. The 'filed = parent' relation was taken from the IMDRF path strings.

My 2025 grid tuning picks the same (0.4, 2, 0.6), and the tuning code never reads 2026. 2026 zero-shot (right / false a year, sampled false): Qwen 123 / 9,052.2 (54), Gemma 149 / 8,690.0 (52), Opus 143 / 2,874.1 (17). But 33 of the 34 are a single pair: Application Security Problem (2 training reports) proposed where Computer System Security Problem (4 training reports) was filed. corrections: The veto does not require that the nearest reports are 'nearly all' one frequent code. It requires at least 2 neighbours at cosine >= 0.4, none carrying the proposed code, and the most common known code frequent with a share >= 0.6.

On 2026 the reductions are 38-57% of false rare answers (Qwen 38%, Gemma 40%, Opus 57%) at a cost of 6-7% of right ones. On the 2025 tuning year the same rule cost 15-21% of right answers (Qwen 201 to 159, Gemma 165 to 141, Opus 175 to 149). Report the cost as year-dependent.

Freshness: the 2024-vs-2025 memory gap comes almost entirely from one insulin-pump template, Failure to Reset filed as Pumping Stopped. Its rows have top cosine 0.17-0.35 in the 2024 pool and 0.31-0.54 in the 2025 pool. This sampled-row breakdown accounts for 10 of the 12 rows only the 2025 memory removes for Opus, 8 of about 14 for Qwen and 11 of about 18 for Gemma. Write 'a template that appeared in 2025 needs fresh memory', not 'filing habits drift'.

What the veto leaves is not 'often the rare child of a filed parent'. Of Opus's 17 kept sampled false answers, 15 are in another IMDRF family and 1 is a parent case; Qwen has 6 of 54 and Gemma 3 of 52 parent cases. 5 of Opus's 17 are still the Failure to Reset template, so they are not one-off either.

Second-look '34 of 63 child-of-filed-parent': 33 of these are one pair (Application Security Problem proposed, Computer System Security Problem filed). Both codes are rare (2 and 4 training reports), and all 33 rows are weight-1 census rows. These are rare-vs-rare confusions worth about 33 reports a year. They are not false rare answers on ordinary reports, so the hierarchy-aware-flag lead rests on one code pair.

The second look did separate on 2025 balanced (right kept 65%, false kept 26%). Say 'did not separate on 2026 or 2025nat'. Also, 40 of the 63 false 2026nat checks are census or stratum rows, so they do not represent the uniform-draw false answers.

The planned TF-IDF error key removed 8-17% of zero-shot false answers but 38% of Opus retrieval false answers (3,026 (18) to 1,875 (11)). The exact template key matched 1 sampled 2026 false answer with the all-2025 memory and 3 from 2024val to 2025, so 'never matched across years' is wrong.

The (code, encoder code) numbers for Qwen and Gemma use a memory that adds 2024val, while Opus's use 2025 only. With the same 2025-only memory: Qwen 130 / 9,412 (56), Gemma 157 / 7,891 (47). The memory was also chosen after seeing 2026 (hindsight).
The 57% Opus reduction rests on 23 sampled rows, of which 20 belong to two template clusters. Its uncertainty is larger than a row-level Poisson spread suggests.
check.net: The core numbers are right and free of leakage. I re-implemented the veto and reproduced its 2025-only choice (0.4, 2, 0.6) and every 2026 cell. No sample report key appears in an earlier pool, and the kNN files match a brute-force search. On 2026 the planned veto removes 38-57% of LLM false rare answers at a cost of 6-7% of right ones. On the tuning year the cost was 15-21%, and for Opus 20 of the 23 sampled false answers it removes are two manufacturer templates. Three interpretive claims do not hold. The 'freshness' effect is one 2025 insulin-pump template, not general drift. What the veto leaves is mostly other-family errors, not parent near misses. The second look's 'child of a filed parent' majority is a single rare-vs-rare code pair in the census (about 33 reports a year), which also undercuts the hierarchy-aware lead. The broader conclusion survives the sampling limits: filing memory removes template-driven false rare answers, no planned or hindsight variant gets false answers to or below right ones, and the stacked variants (12-17 sampled false) cannot be told apart from each other or from round 1's rule.

pilots.title: What does the problem look like on raw reports instead of de-duplicated narratives?

report.headline: Counted on raw 2026 reports, rare codes are even rarer than in the pool: 662 of 2,092,273 single-code reports (1 in 3,161), against 552 of 661,160 narratives (1 in 1,198). The reason is that frequent narratives get copied many times while rare ones almost never do: 543 of the 577 rare narratives have exactly one report, and 559 of the 662 rare reports (84%) are the first report of their text, compared with 35% of all reports. An exact-text memory (digits masked) answers 64.8% of raw reports at 96.5% accuracy, which reproduces round 1. On rare codes it adds very little: 56 right rare answers and 9 false ones, a rare precision of 0.86. The coder still has to find 559 rare reports among 736,114 new narratives (1 in 1,317), so the problem a coder faces is the same as in the pool, and "new narrative" is the right unit for judging the coder. Adding the 2024 and 2025 raw files to the memory changes almost nothing (2 more rare reports covered, accuracy down to 0.949). The LLMs' false rare answers are not hidden extra codes or ambiguous filings. In 262 sampled false rare narratives (3 LLMs, zero-shot and retrieval), the rare code the LLM named was never filed for that exact text on any report, single- or multi-code, from 2024 to 2026. The two template families are filed with one frequent code almost every time: the pump "could not be reset" family 1,500 of 1,539 single-code reports as Pumping Stopped, and the pacemaker Code 1003 "high impedance within the battery" family 7,980 of 7,985 as Premature Discharge of Battery. So the filers follow a stable, learnable habit, and the LLM breaks it. Weighting each sampled report by how many reports share its text makes the LLMs look worse, not better: more false rare answers per year, while right rare answers barely move.

leads: A history veto based on near-duplicate templates rather than exact text: before accepting an LLM rare answer, look up earlier filed reports whose text shares the template (for example the first 200 masked characters, or a high-cosine neighbour from the same year so far). Reject the rare answer if that template's filings are consistent (say over 95%) and never include the rare code. Exact text does not catch the template families (pump: 1,547 narratives for 1,562 reports; Code 1003: 2,277 for 8,341), but their filing is 97-99.9% one frequent code. Choose the thresholds on 2025, test on 2026. CPU only, built from the caches in rawstream/raw*.pkl, which would need snippets for all reports (one more pass per zip, about 75 s each).

Re-score the stored outputs counting multi-code reports where any filed code is right. This needs LLM runs on a sample of the 321,793 multi-code 2026 reports (474 carry a rare code): local GPU for Qwen/Gemma (the owner's go-ahead) or API credit for Opus. The finding above says this will not rescue the false rare answers already seen, but it would add rare reports to find (rare codes are 42% multi-code).

A better problem framing to test: a 'new-template detector'. Flag only first-of-narrative reports whose template has no filing history and whose text is far from all training reports, and send those to a human review queue. Rare reports are 84% first-of-narrative; ordinary reports 35%. CPU only (encoder embeddings already cached in runs/maude_encprobs).

Treat Prophylactic removal as a growing code, not an attractor: filings went 11 (2024), 83 (2025), 93 (2026). A prior that is updated online from the filed stream (monthly counts) could tell growing codes from dead ones. CPU only from raw*.pkl; key order is time order (2026 keys all above earlier ones; the dates in the text file are empty).
caveats: The raw scan used the 2026-11-04 device-problem file for all three years. The 2024/2025 pools were built from the 2026-10-06 copy, so a few 2024/2025 codes may differ. The 2026 counts are not affected.

The phrase families were searched only in the first 500 characters of each narrative, so their counts are lower bounds. The in-scan flag 'code 1003' never matched because digits were masked first; the pacemaker family was found through 'high impedance within the battery'.

The memory assumes each earlier report's filed code is known when the next copy arrives, and uses report-key order as time order. The DATE_REPORT field is empty in all three text files, so key order could not be checked against dates; it is only known that the 2026 keys all follow the 2024/2025 keys.

The report-level (n_reports) yearly counts come from the uniform draw and are very noisy. One row stands for 909 reports, and the uniform draw's report-count estimate (1.51M) overshoots the real pool total (1.10M). Sampled counts are given next to each yearly count.

The combined memory-plus-coder false rare counts are estimates (pool rate per narrative times the number of new narratives); no coder was run on the raw stream. Multi-code reports have no LLM outputs, so whether an LLM's rare answer would match one of several filed codes there was not measured directly. It was only shown that the named rare code is never filed for the texts of the sampled false answers.
surprises: The 552 conflict-free rare narratives found in the raw 2026 stream match the pool's 552 exactly, and none of them is filed (single-code) in raw 2024. Rare filings are new text, not repeats.

Across 262 sampled false rare narratives from 3 LLMs and 2 prompt styles, the named rare code was never filed for that text in three years, even as a second code. The false answers are not hidden extra codes.

Prophylactic removal due to corrective action is not a dead code: it was filed 11 times in 2024 and 93 in 2026. Its 2026 filings come largely from a high-flow insufflation sensor template, not from texts that mention 'prophylactic' or 'corrective action'.

Per report the encoder looks far better (0.805 against 0.637) because four Abbott glucose 'erroneous results' templates make up about 2,400 of the draw's 9,169 reports; Opus zero-shot gets them all wrong.
Memory filled with 2024+2025 lowers memory accuracy (0.965 to 0.949): old filings of the same text disagree with 2026 filings.

corrections: Headline 'the LLMs' false rare answers are not hidden extra codes' is overstated: 234 of the 262 sampled false narratives are singletons, filed single-code with the gold code by pool construction, so 'never filed' is automatic for them; only 28 have a second report and 10 have a multi-code copy. The claim holds for the two template families (population counts) and is untested for the rest.

Headline 'weighting by reports makes the LLMs look worse' is refuted: it comes from the w x n_reports estimator, which overstates the frequent-pool report total by 46% (1,499,021 vs 1,028,819). Either direction rests on a few sampled reports (Opus zs 55).
'543 of 577 rare narratives have exactly one report' should read 'exactly one rare report'; 527 have exactly one report of any code.

Template-family counts were lower bounds; on full text the Code 1003 / high-impedance family is 8,391 (phrase) to 10,927 (raw 'code 1003') reports, with 0 'Battery Problem: High Impedance' filings on 357 to 850 multi-code reports, so the conclusion gets stronger.

Their tier() puts zero-training-count codes into '6-20'; the true 6-20 multi-code share is 0.221 (2,617/11,830), not 0.195.
'Rare filings are new text, none in raw 2024' is mostly true by construction (pool drops 2024-pool texts); not a finding about filers.
Memory-first also overwrites 47 of the 103 rare reports it answers with a non-rare code; the headline mentions only its 9 false rare answers.
check.net: The raw-stream census numbers all reproduce from an independent scan: 662 rare of 2,092,273 single-code reports (1 in 3,161), 559 of 662 rare reports first of their text against 35% overall, and the pool's 552 rare items matching key for key. An exact-text memory answers 64.8% of reports at 96.5% but adds only 56 right rare answers (9 false). So 'new narrative' is a sound unit for judging the coder, with rare reports about 1 in 1,316 among new texts. The template evidence holds and gets stronger on full text: the pump and Code 1003 families are filed 97-99.7% under one frequent code, and the LLMs' rare code is filed essentially never, even on hundreds of multi-code copies. The two broader headline claims do not survive. 'Never filed for any of 262 false narratives' is true by construction for the 234 singletons and rests on 10 multi-code cases. 'Report weighting makes LLMs look worse' comes from an estimator that overstates the report total by 46%; a ratio estimator gives the same or lower per-report false counts. Both of those claims also sit inside the 164-reports-per-sampled-row noise.

leads: Run V5-style conventions as a pipeline rather than a prompt (CPU only). Mine 2025 for phrase -> filed-code rules with high filing purity (as in notes_evidence.json) and apply them as a post-hoc override on the stored 2026 zs answers over the full natural sample. This scores all 3,974 uniform rows instead of 43 F items and avoids agent drift.

Test whether the V5 effect generalises beyond the targeted templates (CPU, plus Opus agents for coding). Build notes from 2024 only, score them on 2025 F-type items, and count how many 2025 false rare answers have no matching note. That share bounds what conventions can fix.

Get the U bound down (Opus agents, CPU). Run V2 and V5 on 500-1,000 more uniform rows; at 0/1,000 the bound on new false rare answers drops to about 2,400 a year. Required before any claim that V5 adds no false answers.

Re-run V0 a second time on the same 233 items (Opus agents). This measures the agent's own test-retest agreement, which separates prompt effects from batch-context noise (V0 already drifts on 22% of items).

Treat the recall problem separately (CPU). Every variant recovers at most 2/30 RM items, so the missed rare codes need either retrieval of 2026 examples or acceptance that they are out of reach for zero-shot coding.

surprises: V2 removed false rare answers and right rare answers in nearly the same proportion: F rare 32 -> 14 of 40, RR 50 -> 19 of 60. Stating frequencies in the prompt behaves like a blunt threshold, not a prior that helps discrimination.

V0 itself lost 10 of the 60 stored-right RR items. 4 of them are Radiofrequency Interference (RFI) reports answered with Electromagnetic Interference, so the agent setup is a little less willing to name rare codes than the bare API call.

V1 used the top-level abstain term 'Adverse Event Without Identified Device or Use Problem' on 6 ordinary U reports whose filed code was Patient Device Interaction Problem or similar. Given an abstain option, the model uses it on patient-reaction reports.

result.reading: The false rare answers have two separable causes, and they need different fixes. (1) A few literal templates whose filing habit is stable and learnable: pump 'could not be reset' is filed 1,500 of 1,539 times as Pumping Stopped, and Code 1003 'high impedance within the battery' 7,980 of 7,985 times as Premature Discharge. These make up 20 of the 23 Opus rows the filing veto removes and 25 of the 43 F items. Telling the model the convention (V5) fixes 24 of the 25. (2) A diffuse remainder with no template, where frequency cues do discriminate. I re-scored the stored prompt-test answers (scratchpad/stab.py). On the 15 non-template zero-shot-false F items, V2 keeps the rare code on 1/15 (7%), against 19/60 (32%) on right rare answers. Requiring V0 and V1 to agree keeps 3/15 (20%), against 41/60 (68%). V2's 'blunt' look in round 2 came from the 13/25 template items it could not fix. These are post-hoc splits on n=15, so they are leads, not results. Recall is a separate problem that no prompt touches: RM recovered 2/30, and the ceiling is 219/552. The misses are codes that grow inside the year, so only fresh filed examples can reach them. Per-report precision at 1 in 1,198 still looks out of reach: the best plausible stack is about 5-10 false per right answer. So the methods should be judged by how they move the queue's need-200/need-300 and by false answers per right answer at a fixed recall.

ideas.name: Mined filing conventions as a post-hoc override (mechanical V5)
ideas.what: Automate what the 25 hand notes did. From the 2024 pool, mine word 2-4-gram phrases (digits masked) that occur in at least 20 earlier reports, are filed at least 95% under one frequent code, and never under the proposed rare code. Then, for every stored zero-shot or retrieval rare answer, check whether the report contains a phrase whose earlier filings are pure for a frequent code and never the proposed rare code. If so, replace the answer with that frequent code. Tune the purity and support thresholds 2024 -> 2025 and freeze them; then use the 2024+2025 pools as memory for 2026. Score all 3,974 uniform rows plus the census, not 43 items.
ideas.why_it_might_work: V5 converted 24/25 template F items and kept RR at 50/60 (year arithmetic about 155 right / 1,833 false, against 6,665). It also raised U accuracy 46 -> 54/99. The kNN filing veto misses part of the pump template, because those rows have cosine 0.17-0.35 to the 2024 pool. A phrase key does not depend on whole-text cosine. Notes 7 and 9 already show the purity is there in 2024/2025 alone (99.8% and 97.3%). This is not the round-2 veto (top-10 cosine neighbours), and not the exact-text memory (0-1 cross-year matches).
ideas.cheapest_test: CPU only. Use the cached pool texts (wf1/convention/cache_pool_2025.pkl and the 2024 pool, one scan) and the stored arms in rare_limits.load_year. Count Opus zs 2026 right / false a year and the sampled false rows. Do the same for Qwen and Gemma zs, and stacked with the filing veto. Deciding numbers: Opus zs sampled false 40 -> 17 or fewer, at least as good as the veto alone, with right at least 143, and right-loss on 2025 tuning under 10% (the veto cost 15-21% there). Also report the accuracy change on the 3,974 uniform rows; it should rise, as V5's U accuracy did.
