V2 does little on templates (it kept 13/25) but keeps only 1/15 non-template zero-shot-false items, against 19/60 RR. The two together (V2 and V5 both naming the rare code) keep 2/40 F against 19/60 RR. At year scale that is about 333 false / 49 right, against the V5 arithmetic of 1,833 / 155 and round 1's best rule of 873 / 94. The split was found after the fact, so it must be retested on fresh items.
ideas.cheapest_test: Opus agents in the same blinded batch setup as round 2. New items from 2025nat: all uniform rows where stored Opus zs names a rare code (35), 60 RR round-robin, 30 RM, and 500 U to tighten the new-false bound, plus a V0 re-run for drift. Use convention notes built from 2024 only, so that 2025 is out of sample. Deciding numbers: F still rare 4/35 or fewer, with RR kept 25/60 or more. The year false/right ratio should come out below round 1's best rule (873/94, about 9.3).
ideas.needs: API dollars or Opus agents (about 700 items x 2-3 variants); CPU for scoring
ideas.kill_criterion: F still rare more than 8/35, or RR kept under 20/60, or false/right not below 9 at year scale. Also kill if the V0 re-run alone reproduces the separation, which would mean the effect is drift.

ideas.name: Prompt-perturbation agreement as confidence (calibration without log-probabilities)
ideas.what: Run the zero-shot coder K=4 times with small meaning-preserving changes: shuffled label order, the list with restored parents, convention notes on and off. Treat the number of runs that name the same rare code as a confidence score. Use it as a keep rule (for example 3 of 4) and as a queue feature next to the encoder log-probability.
ideas.why_it_might_work: On stored answers (stab.py), requiring V0 and V1 to agree keeps 3/15 non-template false items against 41/60 right ones, a 3.4x separation. V0 against stored zs already drifts on 22% of items. The earlier second look failed because it asked one binary question, with a likelihood ratio of about 1.08. Agreement across runs measures how stable the answer is, which is a different signal. The encoder probability gives AUC 0.80-0.88 but does not fix the template rows, and agreement may add to it.
ideas.cheapest_test: Local Qwen, greedy, with 4 shuffled label orders. Run it only on 2025nat uniform rows where Qwen zs names a rare code (75 sampled), plus the 2025 census rows where it is right (201 a year). That is about 300 reports x 4 runs, under one GPU-hour. Deciding number: keep-rate ratio (right/false) at least 3 with 4 of 4 required, and AUC of the agreement count added to the encoder log-probability for the proposed code, compared with the encoder log-probability alone (0.80-0.88). If it passes, freeze the rule and apply it to 2026nat for Qwen and Gemma.
ideas.needs: Local GPU about 1-2 hours (user go-ahead; shared GPU), or the Opus agent equivalent
ideas.kill_criterion: Keep-rate ratio under 2. Or the AUC added on top of the encoder log-probability is under 0.03. Or greedy decoding gives identical answers under shuffles on more than 95% of rows, so there is no signal.

ideas.name: Rolling same-year filing memory for recall
ideas.what: The coder's memory updates through the year. For each 2026 report, find nearest neighbours among earlier-2026 reports by date (TF-IDF as in errormemory part B), using their filed codes. Propose a rare code when a neighbour at cosine 0.4 or more filed earlier this year carries it. Feed these as candidates and features into the queue.
ideas.why_it_might_work: Only 219 of the 552 rare reports have the filed code in any of the 7 answers, and no prompt recovers RM items (2/30). The missing codes grow inside the year: Computer System Security 16 -> 88, Power Conditioning 5 -> 34 (never named by any coder), Biofilm 2 -> 18. Memory freshness was the strongest single effect in errormemory (2025 memory beat 2024 on 2026). The earlier 'add' rule used only 2024/2025 memory (14 right / 686 false) and cannot see codes that start growing in 2026.
ideas.cheapest_test: CPU only, with wf1/convention/cache_dates2026.pkl and one TF-IDF pass over pool_2026 (cached). Measure (a) how many of the 333 rare reports outside the 7-answer ceiling get their filed code from an earlier-2026 neighbour; (b) false adds on the 3,974 uniform rows; (c) the pooled queue's found at 13,200 (264) and need-300 (25,401), with these candidates added under the frozen lr_full / noatt specification.
ideas.needs: CPU only (about 20-40 minutes)
ideas.kill_criterion: Fewer than 30 rare reports newly reachable beyond the 219, or found at 13,200 rising by fewer than 15 with a paired interval that covers 0.

ideas.name: Cross-fitted code-pair memory plus the veto, as features of a simpler queue
ideas.what: Turn the hindsight (rare code, encoder code) error key into a key fixed in advance. Cross-fit within 2025 by report: learn false and right pairs on one half, guard with right answers from the balanced set and census, evaluate on the other half, then freeze. Add three binary features to the queue's logistic model: filing-veto fires, pair seen false, and convention override fires. Drop the attractor and has_llm features, which the check showed hurt on 2026.
ideas.why_it_might_work: The hindsight key gave Opus zs 154 / 2,390 (14), against the veto's 143 / 2,874 (17), with no right answer lost. Planned tuning could not test it because 2024val has 0 right rare answers. In the queue, removing the attractor and has_llm features cut need-200 from 7,023 to 4,538 (paired -2,471 [-3,964, -1,001]). Veto signals act on exactly the template false proposals that sit high in the queue.
ideas.cheapest_test: CPU only. Reuse queue/qlib.py and errormemory's kNN files. Deciding numbers: per-report Opus zs false 2026 with the cross-fitted key plus the veto, against the veto alone (17 sampled). Queue need-200 and need-300, paired bootstrap against the noatt spec (4,538 / 24,015).
ideas.needs: CPU only
ideas.kill_criterion: The cross-fitted key removes fewer than 3 more sampled false rows than the veto alone, and queue need-200 is not lower than noatt with a paired interval that excludes 0.

ideas.name: Full-length retrieval with filing counts (fixing why retrieval and the second look kept literal codes)
ideas.what: Change the retrieval prompt: show neighbours at full length (no 300-character clip) and add one machine-written line per report, such as 'Earlier reports with this wording were filed as: Premature Discharge of Battery 97% (n=931); Battery Problem: High Impedance 0'. The line comes from the phrase table of idea 1. Keep a single coding call; do not add a separate verify call.
ideas.why_it_might_work: Opus retrieval kept High Impedance on 13 of 13 even though 9.9 of 10 neighbours carried the filed code. The clip removed the decisive sentence: 'impedance' first appears at character 274, and the examples were cut at about 300. The second look kept the literal code 28 of 32 times under the same clip. V5 shows that telling the model the convention works. This is the automatic, list-free version, and it covers notes that nobody wrote by hand.
ideas.cheapest_test: Opus agents or API on the 18 Opus rag-false 2026 uniform rows, 60 RR, 30 RM and 100 U, paired against stored rag. Deciding number: High Impedance converted on at least 10 of 13, rag-false still rare 6/18 or fewer, RR loss 5 or fewer.
ideas.needs: API dollars or Opus agents (about 210 items); CPU for the phrase table
ideas.kill_criterion: Fewer than 10/13 High Impedance rows converted with full text and counts, or more than 5 RR lost. Either would mean that literal reading outweighs shown filing evidence, and the mechanical override (idea 1) should be the only route.

ideas.name: Cheap fresher encoder (2024+2025 data) for gate and queue
ideas.what: Retrain the RoBERTa encoder, or as a CPU stand-in a TF-IDF plus class-balanced linear model, on 2024 and 2025 filed reports, then rebuild the gate and the queue features. A deployable system would retrain every year anyway.
ideas.why_it_might_work: The encoder is the queue's backbone: encoder mass alone finds 182 at 13,200, and the encoder probability of the proposed code gives AUC 0.80-0.88. But it has only seen 2024. Fresh memory beat stale memory on 2026 (veto: 2,873 against 4,844 Opus false). The encoder gate holds only 305 of the 552 rare reports, and the misses are new habits.
ideas.cheapest_test: CPU first. Fit a TF-IDF plus logistic model (class-balanced) on 2024 alone and on 2024+2025, and score 2026nat plus balanced. Compare rare mass inside the 7% gate (rare reports held: 305 of 552) and encoder-only need-200 (16-17k). Go to the GPU RoBERTa retrain only if the CPU fresh/stale gap is at least 30 rare reports.
ideas.needs: CPU for the stand-in; local GPU for a few hours for the real retrain (user go-ahead)
ideas.kill_criterion: The fresher CPU model gains fewer than 30 rare reports in the gate, or under 10% on encoder-only need-200, over the 2024-only CPU model.

top3: Mined filing conventions as a post-hoc override (CPU, scores the whole uniform draw, directly tests whether V5's 24/25 template fix generalises without hand notes)

Frequency-plus-convention prompt (V2+V5) on fresh 2025 items: post-hoc split shows V5 fixes templates and V2 fixes the non-template remainder (other-F kept 1/15 vs RR 19/60), joint about 333 false / 49 right a year
Rolling same-year filing memory for recall (CPU): the only lever aimed at the 333 rare reports no coder or prompt reaches (RM 2/30)
do_not_bother: Another binary LLM second look or verifier call (likelihood ratio about 1.08; kept literal codes 28/32). Only retry with full text and filing counts inside the coding call (idea 6).
Frequency counts alone in the prompt as a fix (V2 alone cut right answers 50 -> 19 of 60). Use it only combined with conventions.
More list edits on Opus (V1: F 32 -> 25 of 40, cost 6 RR, abstain labels on 13/100 U). Prophylactic and abstain edits matter for Qwen/Gemma volume, but the per-report ratio stays 10x or worse.
Rogan-Gladen, BBSE or EM counting at this prevalence.
Template-bundle review (13-27% of false volume in bundles of 10 or more).
Hierarchy-aware parent scoring (the 34/63 near misses are one rare-vs-rare code pair, about 33 reports a year).
Exact-text cross-year template memory (0-1 cross-year matches) and the attractor feature in the queue (it hurt need-200 by about 2,500).
Agreement of the three LLMs as a cleaner (they share attractors and fail on the same reports).

result.reading: The original goal, one trusted leaf code per report with rare codes right more often than wrong, cannot be reached at 1 in 1,198. Every corrected rule, list repair, memory veto and prompt variant still leaves 6 to 47 false rare answers for each right one, and counting gives no way around it. What the rounds keep finding is not random LLM error. It is structured disagreement between what the text says and how a template is filed. Code 1003 is filed as Premature Discharge on 7,980 of 7,985 reports, the pump template as Pumping Stopped on 1,500 of 1,539, and once the model is told the convention (V5) it fixes 24 of 25 such items and gains ordinary accuracy (9 vs 1, p=0.021). At the same time, filing habits move between years with no change in the text: Priming vs Filling, Implant subsidence 7 to 86, Pyxis as Medication Error, Medication Error 156 to 78 while the LLMs keep reading flow problems. So the three coders are most useful as instruments, not labellers. The encoder has learned the conventions, the zero-shot LLM reads the text literally and knows no conventions, and retrieval sits in between. Where they disagree, that disagreement measures convention. The one missing fact that decides whether that is worth anything is whether a human finds the literal code defensible. Round 1's readers were Opus-family and side with Opus about 85% of the time on any disagreement, so the 25 of 25 does not count. No human has read anything yet.

ideas.name: Human calibration of the convention gap (gate for every reframe below)
ideas.what: Before building any discrepancy product, one person decides whether 'text says X, filed Y' is a real gap or LLM misreading. Who it serves: whoever acts on a discrepancy flag (a regulator analyst, a manufacturer QA team). The coders give, for free, the exact items to read: the 43 F items of 2026nat (25 in the two template families, 18 others), the G5 frequent-code disagreements from round 1's audit, and the 2025 notes evidence (notes_evidence.json).
ideas.why_it_might_work: Everything downstream depends on this, and the only evidence so far is confounded. Round 1's readers backed Opus's rare code on 36 of 43 G1 items, but also on 35 of 40 ordinary disagreements (G5), so they agree with Opus whatever it says. Qwen and Gemma false rare answers were backed only 17-18 of 40. The template texts state the rare code's wording outright ('high impedance within the battery'), and filers use the frequent sibling 97-99.9% of the time.
ideas.cheapest_test: About 60 items, blinded and shuffled, read by the user or a device-safety colleague. Each item shows the two candidate codes with their IMDRF definitions (from deviceproblemcodes.zip), A/B order randomised and no source shown: 20 template-family F items, 18 non-template F items, 22 G5 ordinary disagreements. Answers: 'filed better / candidate better / both acceptable'. CPU prep from wf2/coder_key/items.pkl and the round-1 audit prep; about 1.5 human hours. Decisive numbers: the share of template items where the reader says 'candidate better or both acceptable', compared with the same share on G5.
ideas.needs: CPU only + about 1.5 human hours
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill the convention-gap ideas (the register, the manufacturer audit and the second-code idea) if the human prefers the filed code on 14 or more of the 20 template items, or if the template share is not at least 25 points above the G5 share. The 'false' rare answers are then plain LLM error, and the queue becomes the only product.

ideas.name: Template-family convention-gap register (the disagreement as the product)
ideas.what: A ranked list of text families, not single reports, whose filed code is stable and differs from what all three LLMs read in the text. For example, 'Code 1003 / high impedance within the battery': 8,341 reports, filed 99.9% Premature Discharge, read as Battery Problem: High Impedance by all three LLMs. Each entry gives the family size, the filed-code purity, the LLM consensus code, sample texts and the year it first appeared. A regulator uses it to review whether a manufacturer's habit hides a failure mechanism (battery impedance vs early depletion); a manufacturer uses it to check its own template. The coders give for free: consensus of the three zero-shot LLMs (overlap 22-35x chance, nearly always the same code), plus the encoder's filed-code prediction as the 'convention' side.
ideas.why_it_might_work: False rare answers concentrate: the top 5 codes carry 69-85%, and the attractors persist from 2025 to 2026 (Spearman 0.52-0.78). The two families make 25 of Opus's 40 sampled false answers and have very high filing purity (rawstream). Bundling failed only as a way to clear false volume (13-27% sits in groups of 10 or more). A register needs only the top entries, so that failure does not apply. The 2025 notes already found 25 such regularities with 71-100% purity.
ideas.cheapest_test: CPU. On 2025nat uniform rows plus 2024val (Qwen, Gemma), take rows where at least 2 of the 3 zero-shot answers agree on a code different from the filed one. Cluster them by TF-IDF cosine at 0.5 or above on the masked text, coarser than the 200-character prefix that split Code 1003 into 4 or more groups. For each cluster, estimate its year size and filed purity from cache_pool_2025.pkl / pools_2024_2025.pkl. Freeze the top 20 by year size times purity on 2025. Then check 2026 (pool_2026 and 2026nat outputs): how many of the 20 recur with purity of 90% or more and the same LLM consensus code. Give the human reader 10 entries under the protocol of the calibration idea.
ideas.needs: CPU only (+ about 0.5 human hour if the calibration passes)
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill if fewer than 10 of the 20 2025 entries recur in 2026 with the same consensus and filed code (unstable, not a register), or if, after the calibration, fewer than 4 of 10 entries are judged a real gap, meaning the list is mostly parent/child near-synonyms an analyst would dismiss.

ideas.name: Filing-habit change detector: same text, new code
ideas.what: Alert when a stable text family's filed-code distribution shifts between periods. Who it serves: an analyst who needs to know that a count jump comes from relabelling, not from new failures, and a researcher whose trend series break silently. The coders give, for free, a convention-free reader. The zero-shot answer distribution on the family should stay put when only the habit changed, and move when the content changed. That separates 'habit drift' from 'new problem'.
ideas.why_it_might_work: Known habit changes exist and broke every estimator: Priming vs Filling went from 97% Filling in 2024 to 65% Priming in 2025; 'subsided' moved to Implant subsidence (7 to 86); Pyxis reports became Medication Error in 2025; battery-cap contacts fell to 8% Power Problem in 2025. In 2026, Medication Error fell from 156 to 78 while the LLMs read those reports as flow problems, and Power Conditioning rose from 5 to 34 without any coder ever naming it. The filing-memory veto lost most of its power with 2024 memory because one pump template moved. Counting failed because rates move; this turns the moving rates into the signal.
ideas.cheapest_test: CPU on the cached 2024 and 2025 pools (wf2/notes/pools_2024_2025.pkl). Group reports into masked-text families (TF-IDF cosine 0.6 or above, or a 120-character skeleton) that have at least 30 reports in both years. Rank by Jensen-Shannon divergence of the filed-code distribution, with a binomial floor against small groups. Pre-set test: are at least 3 of the 4 known 2025 shifts (Priming, Implant subsidence, Pyxis, battery cap) in the top 50? Then read the top 50 quickly and count real shifts. Freeze the method and run 2025 to 2026 once, checking Medication Error and Security.
ideas.needs: CPU only
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill if fewer than 2 of the 4 known shifts are in the top 50, or if fewer than 20 of the top 50 are real habit shifts (the rest small-group noise), which is more alerts than an analyst would read.

ideas.name: Manufacturer convention audit via encoder-vs-zero-shot gap
ideas.what: Per manufacturer within a product code, measure how much correct coding depends on learned convention. That is the share of reports where the encoder, which learned the conventions, gets the filed code and the zero-shot LLM, which reads literally, does not, compared with other manufacturers of the same product code. Who it serves: a regulator comparing filers, and a manufacturer checking whether its template departs from peers. The coders give it for free: the gap between the encoder and zero-shot accuracy, per row.
ideas.why_it_might_work: The template families are single-manufacturer: Tandem for the pump, Boston Scientific for Code 1003. The encoder gives the filed code on 31 of Opus's 40 false rare answers. The heaviest copied narratives (Abbott glucose 'erroneous results', 909 reports) are right for the encoder and wrong for Opus zero-shot. So the encoder-zero-shot gap looks like a convention marker that clusters by manufacturer.
ideas.cheapest_test: CPU on 2024 only: 2024val (10,000 rows, Qwen and Gemma zero-shot outputs) joined with manufacturer and product_code from pool.jsonl / device2024.zip. Fit a logistic model of the gap indicator on product code, then add manufacturer, and run a likelihood-ratio test with a permutation null. Rank manufacturer x product-code cells by excess gap. Decisive: does manufacturer add signal after product code, and are Tandem and Boston Scientific pacing in the top 10?
ideas.needs: CPU only (2024 only; 2025/2026 manufacturer fields would need the FDA DEVICE files, a download that needs the user's OK)
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill if manufacturer adds nothing after product code (permutation p > 0.05), or if the top cells are tiny (fewer than 30 rows) and do not include the known template manufacturers.

ideas.name: Auto-mined convention book: a published rule set and a post-hoc override
ideas.what: Turn V5's hand-written notes into automatically mined phrase-to-filed-code rules with held-out purity. The book is both a deliverable (a de facto coding guide per template) and a cheap override for any coder. Who it serves: a manufacturer coding its own filings consistently, and any coder (LLM or human) that lacks the conventions. The coders give for free where to mine: the zero-shot vs filed disagreements point to the phrases whose convention is non-literal.
ideas.why_it_might_work: V5 converted 24 of 25 template F items, kept right rare answers at 50 of 60 and raised ordinary accuracy from 46 to 54 of 99 (paired 9 vs 1). The 2025 notes held 92-100% purity on several phrases across 2024 and 2025. The filing-memory veto removed 57% of Opus false answers, mostly the same two templates. What differs from the veto: rules assign a positive code to every report (not only rare vetoes), they are mined without hand selection, and they are scored as a guide on held-out filings.
ideas.cheapest_test: CPU. Mine candidate n-gram rules (3-6 grams on masked text) from the 2024+2025 pools: support of 30 or more, filed purity of 95% or more, and not matching any true rare-code report in 2024/2025. Apply once to pool_2026: coverage of 2026 narratives, 2026 purity per rule, and the change in accuracy and false-rare count when the rules override stored Opus/Qwen/Gemma zero-shot answers on 2026nat uniform rows. Compare with the 200-character template memory, which covered 13-16% at about 0.9.
ideas.needs: CPU only
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill if the rules do not beat template-memory coverage by 5 points at equal accuracy, or if median 2026 purity is below 85% (conventions drift faster than a yearly book).

ideas.name: Hierarchical output that stays general when the coders disagree
ideas.what: Emit the lowest common ancestor of the coders' answers (encoder, retrieval, zero-shot), or the deepest node where at least 2 agree, instead of always a leaf. Who it serves: a researcher counting failure modes by family, who gains more from a right family than a wrong leaf. This differs from the killed 'lenient scoring': the output depth changes, and it is scored exactly at the depth emitted, against the encoder truncated to the same depth.
ideas.why_it_might_work: False rare answers cross IMDRF families 65-73% of the time, so a lowest-common-ancestor rule collapses most of them to the root (abstain) automatically. Level-1 accuracy is already 0.816 (encoder) and 0.82-0.83 (retrieval) in 2026, against 0.64 exact. Most of the top 20 confused pairs are one level apart or siblings. Sibling confusion made group counts follow the Security rise better than single codes did.
ideas.cheapest_test: CPU on stored arms. Freeze the rule on the 2025 uniform rows, then score 2026 uniform rows: precision at the emitted node, mean emitted depth, and the share of root abstains. Baseline: the encoder truncated by its own top probability to the same depth distribution (matched coverage-specificity curve). Paired bootstrap over the 3,974 rows. Also report rare leaves emitted, right vs false.
ideas.needs: CPU only
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill if, at matched mean depth, precision does not beat the encoder truncation (bootstrap interval includes 0). The encoder alone would then be the hierarchical product, and the LLMs would add nothing to it.

ideas.name: Second-code suggestion (only if the calibration says the gap is real)
ideas.what: Keep the filed code and attach the LLM's literal code as a suggested secondary code, for example Premature Discharge plus Battery Problem: High Impedance. Who it serves: a regulator searching by mechanism. The coders give it for free: the zero-shot answer whenever it differs from an encoder answer that matches the filed code.
ideas.why_it_might_work: Rare codes are filed on multi-code reports 42% of the time, against 26% for frequent codes, so filers do use second codes for rare mechanisms. The literal readings are consistent across the three LLMs.
ideas.cheapest_test: First a CPU check on raw 2026: for multi-code reports that carry a rare code (474), how often is the second code a literal-text reading of the narrative (phrase match to the label words)? Then Opus agents code about 200 multi-code reports, and we score whether the LLM answer hits a non-primary filed code.
ideas.needs: CPU, then about 200 agent codings (API credit or local GPU, with the user's go-ahead)
ideas.kill_criterion: Already weak: Battery Problem: High Impedance appears 0 times on 337-850 multi-code Code 1003 copies, so filers do not use it as a second code. Kill if the LLM answer matches a non-primary filed code on fewer than 10% of multi-code reports, or if the calibration fails.

top3: Human calibration of the convention gap. It costs about 1.5 human hours and decides whether every disagreement product lives or dies. No human has read anything yet, and the Opus-family readers are confounded (they back Opus about 85% of the time even on ordinary disagreements).

Template-family convention-gap register. CPU only. It uses the attractor concentration and the near-pure filing of the Code 1003 and pump families (99.9% and 97%), and it needs only stable top entries, not the volume clearance that bundling failed at.

Filing-habit change detector. CPU on cached pools, with four known 2025 shifts as a pre-set yardstick. It turns the year-to-year rate drift that broke every counting estimator into the signal, and it tells relabelling apart from new problems.
do_not_bother: More per-report rare-leaf labelling rules, list repairs or prompt variants aimed at false fewer than right. V1 and V2 failed, V5 reaches only about 12 false per right, and the 2025-pruned list reaches 6.7-26x. The base rate settles it.

Corrected counting (Rogan-Gladen, BBSE, EM, PPV/FOM) of rare or family totals. MAUDE gives the filed counts for free. The estimators that come near the truth mostly carry last year's rate over, and the false-alarm rate is not stable between years (Gemma 136 to 219 per 10,000).
More Opus-family blinded readers as the arbiter of whether a filed code is wrong. They agree with Opus about 85% of the time, rare or not.
Rare-code alerting from raw LLM output counts. Opus's Security group output rose about 24x against a true 5.5x, Power Conditioning is never named, and Medication Error moved the other way.

Bundled review of false proposals to clear volume. 73-87% of the false volume sits outside groups of 10 or more same-opening reports. Use families only for the register, where the top entries are what count.
Hierarchy-aware flags built on the second-look 'child of filed parent' cases. 33 of the 34 are a single rare-vs-rare pair.

result.reading: Gold is free. Every report carries its filed code, so measuring a rule against the filed code never needs an annotator. The only scarce resource is coder outputs on enough ordinary reports. Each of the 3,974 uniform rows stands for 164 reports a year, which is why rules at 380-870 false a year (2-5 sampled) cannot be told apart. The encoder gate is a poor stratifier for false answers, but the local LLMs are a strong one. In the cached arms (computed now), the gate holds 9 of Opus zs's 40 sampled 2026 false rare answers (3 of 35 in 2025). The flag 'Qwen or Gemma zs names any rare code' covers 3.4% (2.6% in 2025) of ordinary reports. It holds 35 of 40 (28 of 35) Opus zs false answers, 16 of 18 (11 of 11) Opus rag false answers, and 84 of 92 (105 of 109) of Opus zs's right rare answers in the natural census. So the cheap honest route has three parts: a big fresh uniform draw coded by a local LLM in one or two GPU nights (Qwen zs about 0.6 s and Gemma zs about 1.0 s per report, from the stored run timings), Opus run only on the reports the local LLMs flag, and rules defined to fire only inside that flag, so their false side is fully counted. Human reading is only needed for one separate question: is the filed code defensible where the LLM disagrees with it? That needs a small calibrated panel, and it should not be mixed into the counting.

ideas.name: Fresh local-LLM uniform draw, month-stratified, frozen rule list
ideas.what: Draw 54,000-72,000 new 2026 ordinary (non-rare-census) narratives uniformly from the same frame the natural sample used: one row per narrative, known codes only, excluding the 3,974 already drawn. Allocate the draw evenly across months by report-key order. Run Qwen zs, and if time allows Gemma zs, plus Qwen rag for the zs==rag rules; retrieval needs neighbour search for the new reports. Before the run, freeze a short list of at most 5-8 candidate rules chosen on 2025: the filing-memory veto (t=0.4, m=2, s=0.6), veto plus zs==rag, prior-corrected, the best round-1 rules and the V5-style phrase overrides mined from 2025. Score them once. This gives a fresh test set that none of the hindsight choices has touched.
ideas.why_it_might_work: Each current uniform row weighs 164. With 3,974 + 54,000 rows the weight drops to about 11.3 a year per row. Qwen zs false (14,693) would rest on about 1,300 sampled answers (±5%). A rule at 870 false would rest on about 77 (±22%), and one at 380 on about 34 (95% Poisson 23-47, so about 260-530 a year, against today's roughly 40-1,190). Zero observed would bound false at about 34 a year, against about 600 today. Throughput is measured from stored runs: Qwen zs 0.58-0.61 s a report (about 6,000 an hour), Gemma zs about 1.0 s, Qwen rag about 1.05 s. So 12 hours gives about 72k Qwen zs only, or about 27k Qwen+Gemma zs. Two nights give about 54k with both. The labels cost nothing, because the filed code is the gold.
ideas.cheapest_test: Pilot of 2,000 new reports with Qwen zs (about 20 minutes). Check that throughput is at least 4,000 an hour, that 0 answers are unparseable beyond the stored rate, and that the share of reports with a rare answer is 1.5-3% (stored: 2.2% in 2026). Then run the full night. Deciding number: the 95% interval for each frozen rule's false count a year. Success means at least one pair of rules whose intervals do not overlap, or a rule whose upper bound sits below 3x its (exact) right count.
ideas.needs: Local GPU, one or two nights (about 12-24 GPU-hours), with the user's go-ahead. CPU for drawing the frame, building retrieval neighbours (or a short GPU job) and scoring.
ideas.kill_criterion: Stop if the pilot shows a rare-answer rate outside 1.5-3%, which would mean the frame or prompt differs from the stored run. Also stop if, after the full draw, every frozen rule's interval still spans more than 2x. In that case the false volume is too spread for any affordable draw, and the claim should be framed as a bound, not a ranking.

ideas.name: Two-phase: Opus only on the local-LLM flags, with rules defined inside the flag
ideas.what: Phase 1 is the draw above, coded by Qwen and Gemma zs. Phase 2 runs Opus zs, and rag if credit allows, only on the reports where Qwen or Gemma zs named any rare code: 2.6-3.4% of ordinary reports, about 1,800 of 54,000. Report Opus rules in a 'flag-restricted' form, where an Opus rare answer counts only if a local LLM also flagged a rare code. Their false side is then a complete count within the draw, with nothing to estimate outside the flag. The unrestricted Opus rules get a residual term estimated from the existing 3,974 + 4,000 (2025) rows, reported separately.
ideas.why_it_might_work: Measured now on the cached arms. The flag holds 35 of 40 (2026) and 28 of 35 (2025) of Opus zs's sampled false rare answers, and 16 of 18 and 11 of 11 of Opus rag's. On the natural census it keeps 84 of 92 (2026) and 105 of 109 (2025) of Opus zs's right rare answers, so restricting costs about 4-9% of right answers. The encoder gate by contrast holds only 9 of 40 and 3 of 35 false answers, about 3x enrichment against about 25x for the flag. Round 1 rejected LLM agreement as a cleaner; here it is used only to make the rules measurable, and its cost in right answers is known exactly from the census. Interval: with 54k phase-1 rows, an Opus rule at 380 false a year rests on about 30 sampled flags (about ±35%), and at 870 on about 70 (±24%).
ideas.cheapest_test: First, on stored data at no cost, score the flag-restricted versions of every round-1/round-2 Opus rule on 2025 and 2026. Confirm they lose at most 10% of right answers and at most 15% of the sampled false answers; measured for raw zs: 8 of 92 right and 5 of 40 false. Then send 300 flagged reports from the first night to the Opus API, zs only, as a cost and parse check, at about $1-2 (inferred). Deciding number: actual dollars per call. Stored usage is about 11,600 cache-read, 130 uncached and 33 output tokens per zs call, and about 1,050 more uncached tokens per rag call. Under Opus-4.5-class prices that is about $0.007 a zs call and $0.013 a rag call, roughly half under batch (an assumption to check). So 1,800 zs calls cost about $7-13, and zs+rag about $18-36.
ideas.needs: API dollars about $10-25 of the $29 (zs certainly, rag if batch pricing holds). Phase-1 GPU time is shared with the uniform-draw idea. CPU for scoring.
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill if the flag-restricted rules lose more than 15% of right rare answers on the census, or if the 300-call pilot costs more than $0.015 a zs call (then 1,800 calls would exhaust the credit). Also kill if Opus answers on 200 re-run stored reports differ from the stored answers on more than 10% of items: then phase-2 answers and the stored 2026 answers are not the same coder.

ideas.name: Full-year encoder pass as the free stratifier and exact encoder baseline
ideas.what: Run the stored cb-large-conv encoder (seed 42) once over all 661,160 2026 narratives, plus 2025 if time allows. Keep the full probability vectors, or at least the top-20 codes and the rare-probability mass. Every encoder-only quantity then becomes a complete count with no sampling error: the encoder rules (today 32 right / 166 false, 1 sampled), the gate size, and the encoder-only queue at every budget, including the 330/660 budgets that the queue pilot could not support. It also gives the stratification variable for the queue census below, and exact monthly encoder rare mass for drift.
ideas.why_it_might_work: The queue pilot showed that the encoder alone is a strong queue (106 found at 3,300 read, 182 at 13,200), but its false side rested on 2-4 sampled ordinary rows at 330/660 and on 19-77 rows at higher budgets. The quant pilot found that encoder probability sums are biased by a near-constant factor (1.47 in 2025, 1.71 in 2026). That is a calibration problem, and only full-year scores can track it. The check already showed that the npz argmax equals the stored encoder answer on 99.4-100% of rows, so the pipeline exists. RoBERTa-large inference is about 1-2 GPU-hours for 661k reports (inferred; check on 10k first). Labels are free, so the result is exact.
ideas.cheapest_test: Encode the 9,741 rows of 2026 + 2026nat that already have stored npz probabilities, plus 10,000 new reports, and time it. Deciding numbers: argmax agreement with the stored npz of at least 99.4%, and extrapolated full-year time of at most 3 GPU-hours. Then run the full year and recompute encoder right/false rare and the encoder-only queue curve. Check that the old estimates (166 false; need-200 about 16-17k) fall inside the old bootstrap intervals.
ideas.needs: Local GPU, about 1-3 hours, with the user's go-ahead. CPU for one scan of pool_2026 (cache the texts in scratch).
ideas.kill_criterion: Stop if the extrapolated time exceeds about 5 GPU-hours, or if argmax agreement on the stored rows is below 99%; in the second case the checkpoint or tokenisation differs and the exact counts would describe a different coder.

ideas.name: Certified census of the queue top for the small budgets
ideas.what: Using the full-year encoder scores, rank all reports by the encoder-only part of a local-LLM queue model (Qwen+Gemma lr_full-style, fitted on 2025 only). Run Qwen zs (and Gemma zs if time allows) on the top 20,000-30,000. For budget B, compute the largest score lift the LLM features can add, from the fitted coefficients and feature ranges. Any report outside the top-K whose encoder-only score plus that lift is below the B-th score cannot enter the read window. Up to the largest certified B, found-at-budget and need-100/200 are then exact counts. Beyond it, the remainder is estimated from the fresh uniform draw.
ideas.why_it_might_work: The queue pilot's numbers at 330/660 read are the count of rare census rows ranked above the 2nd or 4th sampled ordinary row (31, 55, 76, 90 before rows 1-4). Need-100 rests on 3-8 sampled rows. The pilot's check found that specification choices alone move need-200 by about 35%, as much as the bootstrap. A census of the top removes the sampling part, so specification differences become visible. The LLM gain is concentrated at 3,300-13,200 read (+32 to +82), where most of the top is encoder-ranked anyway. Cost: 25k reports x 0.6 s ≈ 4 hours of Qwen zs.
ideas.cheapest_test: On CPU with stored data: fit the Qwen+Gemma queue model on 2025. Compute its maximum LLM-feature lift, and on the 2026 sample find which rows inside the read window for B = 3,300 have an encoder-only score below the K=25,000 cut-off, estimated from the sample's encoder scores. Deciding number: the estimated share of the top-3,300 window that comes from outside the top-25k by encoder-only score. Below 5%: run the census. Above 20%: the certificate will not bind; drop the idea.
ideas.needs: CPU for the feasibility check. Local GPU about 4-8 hours for the census, after the encoder pass.
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill if the largest certified budget is below 1,000 reports read, or if more than 20% of the 3,300-read window comes from outside the census set. Then the small-budget claims still rest on sampled rows, and the honest move is to report only 3,300-13,200 read.

ideas.name: Group-sequential decision on 'false at most c x right', using the asymmetry
ideas.what: Turn each frozen rule's claim into a one-sided test of false a year ≤ c x right, with right known exactly from the census and c = 1 or 2. Process the fresh draw in 10,000-report batches and stop a rule early once its Poisson 95% upper bound falls below c x right (claim holds) or its lower bound rises above it (claim fails). Spread alpha over the frozen rules (Holm). Compare rules in a paired way: count only the reports where they disagree, which for filter rules (veto, overrides) is the set the filter removes.
ideas.why_it_might_work: Arithmetic (inferred). Showing that a rule is bad is cheap, but showing that it is good is expensive. For the Opus rule at 58 right / 380 false, about 10,000 uniform reports give an expected 5.8 sampled false answers with a lower 95% bound of about 2, which is about 131 a year and above 2 x 58. If false were really 58, about 70,000 reports would be needed to push the upper bound below 116. For zero-shot-scale rules with about 150 right, showing false ≤ 300 needs about 30,000 reports. Most candidate rules so far run 6-47x false per right, so most will stop after the first batch, and the GPU night goes to the few close calls. Paired counting helps because the veto's removed set (for example, 23 of 40 Opus zs sampled false answers) is measured directly, not as a difference of two noisy totals.
ideas.cheapest_test: On CPU, simulate the stopping rule with the measured 2026 rates (rule false a year: 380, 873, 2,874, 6,665; right 58-154) to get the expected number of reports until each rule stops, and decide before the run which rules go in. During the run, the deciding numbers are the per-rule stop batch and its verdict.
ideas.needs: CPU only for planning. It schedules the GPU night of the uniform-draw idea and adds no GPU time.
ideas.kill_criterion: If the simulation shows that no frozen rule can reach a verdict of 'holds' within 70,000 reports at c=2, drop the 'good rule' framing and report bounds only. If after 30,000 real reports every rule has stopped as 'fails' at c=3, skip the second night; the question 'is there a usable per-report rare rule' is then answered no.

ideas.name: Calibrated reading panel: LLM readers with decoys, plus a small human double-sample
ideas.what: A separate measurement of whether the filed code or the LLM's code is defensible. It is not used for counting. Strata (about 400 items): (a) the two template families (25 already read), (b) other off-template false rare answers (about 60), (c) ordinary reports at the top of the queue (about 100), (d) right rare answers as controls (about 60), (e) decoys, where the 'proposed' code is a random rare code from another family (about 60), and (f) ordinary reports where the encoder and filed code agree (about 60). Three blinded LLM readers each see the report and the filed and proposed codes in random order, with 'both acceptable' and 'neither' options. The author reads about 80 items, oversampling those where the LLM readers backed the proposed code. Their agreement then corrects the LLM-reader rates (double sampling).
ideas.why_it_might_work: No human has read anything. Round 1's readers backed the literal code 25 of 25 on templates that filers code as Premature Discharge on 7,980 of 7,985 reports. That shows readers measure defensibility, not filing convention. The queue pilot's 'near-synonym' reading rests on 8 rows judged by an agent, and the check found several were not near-synonyms. The decoys measure reader leniency, and without them reader acceptance cannot be interpreted. Intervals: about ±0.11 on a human proportion at n=80, about ±0.10 on LLM-human agreement, and about ±0.07 per LLM-read stratum at n=100 (Wilson).
ideas.cheapest_test: First, 60 decoys plus 60 (d) controls with LLM readers only. Deciding numbers: decoy acceptance and control acceptance. If decoys pass at 10% or less and controls at 85% or more, run the full panel and the author's 80 items, about 1.5-2 hours.
ideas.needs: Opus agents or about $3-6 API (short prompts, about 1,200 reads). About 2 human hours from the author. CPU to build the items from the existing caches.
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill the LLM-reader arm if decoy acceptance exceeds 20% or LLM-human agreement on non-decoys is below 0.7; then report only the human 80 as anecdote-level. Kill the whole panel if the author's reading backs the filed code on at least 90% of strata (a) to (c): the filed code is then the right target and defensibility is not a separate issue.

ideas.name: Time split inside 2026 with exact encoder drift and month-level LLM rates
ideas.what: Use report-key order (and wf1/convention/cache_dates2026.pkl where it applies) to split 2026 into Jan-Apr and May-Oct. Fit the frozen-rule settings, filing memory, phrase overrides and queue model on 2025 plus Jan-Apr 2026, and test them on May-Oct. Compare them with the same rules frozen on 2025 alone. Measure drift on two scales: monthly encoder rare mass and new-template counts, exactly from the full-year encoder pass; and monthly Qwen/Gemma zs false-rare rates from the month-stratified fresh draw, about 5,000-7,000 per month.
ideas.why_it_might_work: The quant pilot found the only established rate shift: Gemma zs went from 136 to 219 per 10,000 between 2025 and 2026 (p = 0.005), with Qwen and Opus within noise. The error-memory pilot found that fresh memory helps because one pump template appeared in 2025. Rolling-memory and online-prior ideas both depend on within-year drift that nobody has measured. At about 5,500 a month, Qwen zs false (about 2.2%) gives about 120 per month (±18%), which detects a 1.5x month-to-month shift. Gemma's 1.6x shift would show in two-month blocks.
ideas.cheapest_test: After the uniform draw exists: a chi-square test of monthly Qwen zs false-rare counts against a constant rate, and the paired difference in May-Oct false counts between 'frozen on 2025' and 'refit on 2025 + Jan-Apr 2026' for the veto and memory rules. Deciding number: whether that paired difference excludes zero.
ideas.needs: CPU only, provided the uniform draw is month-stratified and the encoder pass is done.
ideas.kill_criterion: Kill if monthly rates are consistent with a constant (p > 0.2) and the refit-vs-frozen paired difference covers zero for every rule. Then drift is not a measurement concern at this budget, and plain whole-year counting suffices.

top3: Fresh local-LLM uniform draw (54-72k reports, one to two GPU nights, month-stratified, rule list frozen on 2025 beforehand): about 11 reports a year per sampled row instead of 164, with labels free from the filed code.

Two-phase Opus: run Opus only on the ~3% of reports the local LLMs flag (measured: holds 35/40 and 28/35 of Opus zs false, keeps 84/92 and 105/109 of its right answers), and define rules inside the flag so their false side is a complete count. About $7-25 of the $29.
Full-year encoder pass (about 1-3 GPU-hours): exact encoder baselines and queue curve, plus the stratifier for a certified census of the queue top that settles the 330-3,300 budgets.
do_not_bother: Human annotation of ordinary reports for gold: the filed code is already the gold for every counting question. Human hours belong only in the defensibility panel.

Stratifying by the encoder gate to find LLM false answers: measured, it holds only 9/40 (2026) and 3/35 (2025) of Opus zs's sampled false answers in 5-7% of reports, about 3x enrichment against about 25x for the local-LLM flag.

Running Opus on a bigger uniform draw: at about $0.004-0.007 a zs call (assumed prices), $29 buys at most 4,000-8,000 calls, about one more draw of today's size, which moves weight per row from 164 to about 82 and decides nothing.
Full-year LLM runs (113-247 GPU-hours per LLM per year, from stored timings): the two-phase and certified-census designs give the same answers for 5-10% of the compute.
Rogan-Gladen, BBSE or EM corrections and any 'calibrate on last year' count estimator: the quant pilot showed they need the false-alarm rate stable to about 8 per 100,000, and it is not.
More bootstrap refinement at 330/660 read on the existing 3,974 rows: those claims rest on 2-4 sampled rows, and no resampling scheme adds information.
Comparing further hindsight-chosen rules on the existing 2026 uniform rows: they have been looked at by every pilot. Any new rule must be frozen on 2025 and scored on the fresh draw.

synthesis.is_it_the_problem: Partly. The arithmetic part is real. In 2026 only 552 of 661,160 reports carry a rare code, so a zero-shot LLM that names a false rare code on 1 in 45 (Qwen, Gemma) to 1 in 100 (Opus) ordinary reports produces 6,665-14,693 false rare answers a year against 131-158 right ones. But "over-naming" is not one problem. It has three parts. (1) For Opus, 25 of its 40 sampled false answers come from two manufacturer templates whose text states the rare code's wording, while filers use a frequent code almost every time: the pump template is filed as Pumping Stopped on 1,500 of 1,539 reports, and the Code 1003 template as Premature Discharge on 7,980 of 7,985. That is a gap between filing habit and literal reading, not a random misreading. (2) For Qwen and Gemma, a list artefact dominates: "Prophylactic removal" is the only listed label of a removed family and works as a "no problem" answer (43 of 163 and 64 of 141 sampled false answers). (3) The rest is spread over many codes and families. A second problem matters as much and is untouched: only 219 of the 552 rare reports get the filed code from any of the 7 answers, and no prompt variant recovered missed rare codes (2 of 30).
synthesis.is_it_unavoidable: The base rate is unavoidable. At 1 in 1,198, every tested fix still leaves 6.7 to 47 false rare answers for each right one: the best simple Opus rule is 94 / 873, convention notes (V5) about 155 / 1,833, the filing veto 143 / 2,874, the list-edit upper bound 124-151 / 1,515-5,881, and pruning on 2025 gives 19/504 to 102/682. So rare per-report labels that are mostly right look out of reach with these coders. The measurement limit is also hard: one sampled ordinary report stands for about 164 a year, and 0 sampled still allows about 600. Not unavoidable: the list artefacts (Prophylactic and the children of held-out parents remove an optimistic 37-60% of false volume), the missing filing conventions (V5 fixed 24 of 25 template items and raised ordinary accuracy, 9 gained against 1 lost of 99), and a stale memory (2025 filings beat 2024 filings, though the checker traced that mostly to one pump template). Counting estimators do not escape the base rate. Rates moved between years (Gemma zero-shot 136 to 219 per 10,000, p = 0.005), and the estimators that came near 552 mostly carried last year's rate over.
synthesis.what_solves_it: Nothing tested makes a rare per-report label trustworthy on ordinary reports. What works is changing the output from a label to a ranked review queue. The queue was fitted on 2025, uses the encoder's probability for the proposed code, and pools the three LLMs. On 2026 it finds 200 of the 552 rare reports after about 7,000 reports read (4,500 with an equally pre-set variant that drops the attractor features) and 300 after about 24,000-25,000. The encoder alone needs about 16,000-17,000 and 44,000-54,000, and random reading needs 240,000 and 359,000. Precision is only about 2% at those depths. At small budgets (under about 1,000 read) the queue is no better than the best existing Opus rules, and the sample cannot resolve those budgets anyway. What partly works on the false side: teaching filing conventions, either as prompt notes (V5) or mechanically as the filing-memory veto (which removes 38-57% of false answers at a cost of 6-7% of right answers in 2026, but 15-21% in 2025), and list repair for Qwen and Gemma (untested by re-prompt; on Opus, V1 changed little). What does not work: stating frequencies in the prompt (V2 cut right and false answers alike, 50 to 19 of 60 against 32 to 14 of 40), an LLM second look, agreement among the three LLMs, template bundling, and corrected counting. A better problem is probably not "label each report" but either a review queue for rare reports, or a tool that shows where literal text and filing habit disagree and where filing habits change. Whether the second has value depends on a human judging the literal codes, and no human has read any report yet.

directions.name: Mined filing-convention override (mechanical V5 + veto)
directions.evidence: V5's hand notes fixed 24 of 25 template false items, kept right rare answers at 50 of 60 and raised U accuracy 46 to 54 of 99 (paired 9 vs 1, p=0.021). The kNN filing veto removes 23 of 40 Opus sampled false answers, 20 of them from the two templates, but misses part of the pump template (cosine 0.17-0.35 to 2024). Phrase purity is already high in 2024/2025 (99.8%, 97.3%). V5's notes were built from 2024/2025 only.
directions.next_test: CPU. Mine phrase rules (masked n-grams, support >= 20-30, purity >= 95% for one frequent code, never the proposed rare code, no match in true rare reports) on 2024. Tune thresholds 2024 to 2025 and freeze them; apply to stored 2026 zero-shot and retrieval answers over all 3,974 uniform rows plus the census, alone and stacked with the veto.
directions.needs: CPU only (one cached pass over the 2024 and 2025 pools)
directions.kill_criterion: Removes fewer sampled Opus false answers than the veto (23 of 40), or adds fewer than 3 sampled rows on top of the veto, or costs more than 10% of right rare answers on 2025.

directions.name: Ranked review queue as the product, re-specified and fed with veto/convention features
directions.evidence: Pooled queue finds 200 at about 7,023 read (noatt variant 4,538; paired difference -2,471 [-3,964, -1,001]) and 300 at about 24,000-25,400. The encoder alone needs 16-17k and 44-54k. The LLM gain at 3,300-13,200 read is +32 to +82 rare reports, with paired intervals clear of zero. The speed-up is about 2.3x for 200 and 1.75-2.1x for 300. Precision is about 2% at 13,200. Model specification moves need-200 by about 35%, as much as the bootstrap.
directions.next_test: CPU. Fix the specification without looking at 2026, by cross-fitting within 2025 (by report), choosing between lr_full and noatt plus binary features (veto fires, convention override fires, cross-fitted code-pair memory). Report need-200 and need-300 with paired intervals, and report the specification spread next to the bootstrap. Report only 3,300-13,200 read until the sample grows.
directions.kill_criterion: The cross-fitted queue does not beat the noatt specification on need-200 with a paired interval that excludes 0, and the LLM gain over the encoder-mass queue falls below +30 at 13,200.

directions.name: Human calibration: is the filed code or the literal code defensible?
directions.evidence: No human has read anything. Round 1's Opus-family readers backed Opus on 36 of 43 false rare items but also on 35 of 40 ordinary disagreements (G5), so their 25-of-25 support for the template codes means little. They backed Qwen and Gemma false codes only 17-18 of 40, and Prophylactic 4 of 31. Filers use the frequent code 97-99.9% of the time on the templates.
directions.next_test: About 60-80 items, blinded, with IMDRF definitions and A/B order randomised: 20 template-family F items, 18 non-template F items, 22 G5 ordinary disagreements, plus random-rare-code decoys to measure reader leniency. Answers: filed better / candidate better / both acceptable. Read by the owner or a device-safety colleague, about 1.5-2 hours.
directions.needs: About 1.5-2 human hours; CPU for item prep from wf2/coder_key/items.pkl and the round-1 audit prep
directions.kill_criterion: Kill the convention-gap register and second-code ideas if the human prefers the filed code on 14 or more of the 20 template items, or if the template share is not at least 25 points above the G5 share.

directions.name: Fresh uniform draw coded by local LLMs, with Opus only on local-LLM flags
directions.evidence: Every rule comparison is capped by 164 reports a year per sampled row; rules at 380-870 false rest on 2-5 sampled rows. The filed code is free gold. In cached arms the flag 'Qwen or Gemma zero-shot names any rare code' covers 2.6-3.4% of ordinary reports and holds 35 of 40 (2026) and 28 of 35 (2025) Opus zero-shot false answers, and 84 of 92 and 105 of 109 of its right census answers. The encoder gate holds only 9 of 40 and 3 of 35. Stored timings: Qwen zero-shot about 0.6 s and Gemma about 1.0 s per report.
directions.next_test: Pilot 2,000 new 2026 narratives with Qwen zero-shot (check the rare-answer rate is 1.5-3% and throughput is at least 4,000 an hour). Freeze 5-8 rules on 2025 beforehand. Then run 54-72k reports over one or two nights, month-stratified. Run Opus zero-shot only on the roughly 1,800 flagged reports, after a 300-call cost check.
directions.needs: Local GPU 12-24 hours (shared GPU, owner's go-ahead); API about $7-25; CPU for scoring
directions.kill_criterion: Pilot rare-answer rate outside 1.5-3%, or after the full draw every frozen rule's interval still spans more than 2x. For Opus phase 2: more than $0.015 a call, or more than 10% disagreement with stored answers on 200 re-run reports.

directions.name: Full-year encoder pass (exact encoder baseline and a certified queue top)
directions.evidence: The encoder alone is a strong queue (106 found at 3,300 read, 182 at 13,200), but its false side rests on 2-4 sampled rows at 330/660 and 19-77 rows higher up. The encoder's summed rare probability overshoots by 1.47x (2025) and 1.71x (2026), which only full-year scores can track. npz argmax equals the stored answer on 99.4-100% of rows.
directions.next_test: Time the encoder on the 9,741 stored rows plus 10k new reports (agreement >= 99.4%, extrapolated time <= 3 GPU hours), then score all 661,160 2026 narratives. Recompute the encoder rules and the queue curve exactly, then check whether a Qwen census of the top 20-30k can certify the small budgets.
directions.needs: Local GPU 1-3 hours (owner's go-ahead), then 4-8 hours for an optional top census
directions.kill_criterion: More than about 5 GPU hours, or argmax agreement below 99% on stored rows. For the census: certified budget below 1,000 read, or more than 20% of the 3,300 window from outside the census set.

directions.name: Rolling same-year filing memory for recall
directions.evidence: 333 of 552 rare reports sit outside all 7 answers, and no prompt recovers them (RM 2 of 30). The missing codes grow inside the year: Computer System Security 16 to 88, Power Conditioning 5 to 34 (never named by any coder, though in the list), Biofilm 2 to 18. The add rule using only 2024/2025 memory gave 14 right / 524-686 false. 84% of rare reports are the first report of their text.
directions.next_test: CPU. Using dated 2026 reports (wf1/convention/cache_dates2026.pkl), find TF-IDF neighbours among earlier-2026 filed reports. Count how many of the 333 out-of-reach rare reports get their code from an earlier-2026 neighbour at cosine >= 0.4, and the false adds on uniform rows. Add these as candidates in the frozen queue and measure the found count at 13,200.
directions.kill_criterion: Fewer than 30 newly reachable rare reports, or fewer than 15 more found at 13,200 with a paired interval covering 0.

directions.name: Filing-habit change detector and convention-gap register
directions.evidence: Known habit shifts with unchanged text: Priming vs Filling (97% Filling in 2024, 65% Priming in 2025), 'subsided' to Implant subsidence (7 to 86), Pyxis to Medication Error, battery-cap contacts. Medication Error fell 156 to 78 while the LLMs read those reports as flow problems. The template families are single-manufacturer and near-pure, and false rare answers concentrate (top 5 codes carry 69-85%, persisting from 2025 to 2026).
directions.next_test: CPU on the cached 2024/2025 pools. Form masked-text families with at least 30 reports in both years and rank them by divergence of the filed-code distribution. Pre-set check: are at least 3 of the 4 known 2025 shifts in the top 50? For the register, freeze the top 20 LLM-consensus vs filed-code families on 2025 and check how many recur in 2026.
directions.needs: CPU only; the register's value also depends on direction 3
directions.kill_criterion: Fewer than 2 of the 4 known shifts in the top 50, or fewer than 20 of the top 50 real shifts. Register: fewer than 10 of 20 entries recur in 2026, or the human calibration fails.

directions.name: Re-prompt with list repair plus conventions on fresh items (Qwen/Gemma list repair; V2+V5 merged for Opus)
directions.evidence: For Qwen and Gemma, the optimistic bound for removing Prophylactic and the children of held-out parents is 39-60% of false volume, but nobody has re-prompted them. On Opus, V1 changed little (F 32 to 25 of 40, and abstain labels on 13 of 100 U). A post-hoc split suggests V2 suppresses non-template false items (1 of 15 kept, against 19 of 60 right) and V5 fixes templates. Jointly that is about 333 false / 49 right a year, from n=15, found after the fact.
directions.next_test: On 2025nat items, with notes built from 2024 only: Opus agents run V0 (re-run for drift), V5, and V2+V5 on 35 F, 60 RR, 30 RM and 500 U items. Separately, run Qwen and Gemma with the repaired list on the 8,000 uniform rows of 2025nat and 2026nat.
directions.needs: Opus agents or API (about 700 items x 2-3 variants); local GPU a few hours for Qwen/Gemma (owner's go-ahead)
directions.kill_criterion: Opus: F still rare on more than 8 of 35, or RR kept below 20 of 60, or false/right not below 9 at year scale, or the V0 re-run alone shows the same separation. Qwen/Gemma: false rare volume falls by less than 25% on the uniform rows.

dead: Per-report rare-code labels that are mostly right at natural proportions, from any current coder, rule, list edit, memory veto or prompt variant (best is about 6.7x false per right).

Corrected counting of rare or family totals: Rogan-Gladen, BBSE, EM (Saerens) on encoder probabilities. Estimators that came near 552 carried last year's rate over; copying last year's rate gives 518 with no coder.
Stating label frequencies alone in the prompt (V2): it suppresses right and false rare answers alike.
An LLM second look or verifier call as currently built (likelihood ratio about 1.08; kept literal codes 28 of 32, and 14 of 17 on right ones too).
Agreement of the three LLMs as a cleaner (they share attractors; 99 right / 2,977 false).
Encoder top-1 disagreement as a veto (kills 129 of Opus's 154 right rare answers).
Template-bundle review to clear false volume (73-87% of false volume is outside groups of 10 or more).
Hierarchy-aware 'child of filed parent' flag (33 of the 34 cases are one rare-vs-rare code pair, about 33 reports a year).
Exact-text cross-year template memory as a veto (0-1 cross-year matches); exact-text memory adds only 56 right rare answers on the raw stream.
Raw LLM output counts as a new-habit alarm (Opus Security group overshoots 24x, Power Conditioning never named, Medication Error moved the other way).
Richer candidate lists to raise the recall ceiling (perfect chooser 243 to at most 297 of 552).
Lenient parent/sibling scoring as a fix for the false side.
Claims at 330/660 read on the existing 3,974 uniform rows (2-4 sampled ordinary rows), and further hindsight rule picking on those rows.
needs_owner_decision: Human reading: about 1.5-2 hours for the blinded calibration panel (filed code vs literal code, with decoys). Nothing downstream on the convention-gap reading can be settled without it.

GPU time on the shared GPU: full-year encoder pass (1-3 hours), fresh local-LLM uniform draw (12-24 hours over one or two nights), optional queue-top census (4-8 hours), Qwen/Gemma re-prompt with the repaired list (a few hours).

API money: Opus on the roughly 1,800 local-LLM flagged reports (about $7-25 under assumed prices, checked first with a 300-call pilot), and Opus prompt variants on about 700 fresh items if agents are not used. The available credit is unclear: memory says about $78 left and also that the API credit expired on 11-05; the measurer lens assumed $29.
Downloads: FDA DEVICE files for 2025/2026 manufacturer fields, only if the manufacturer-level convention audit is pursued.
Framing choice: whether the target stays 'one leaf code per report' or moves to a review queue, a convention-gap register, or a habit-change detector.
open_contradictions: Are the template 'false' answers errors at all? Filers use the frequent code 97-99.9% of the time, and Opus-family readers back the literal code 25 of 25, but those readers back Opus about 85% of the time on any disagreement. Unresolved until a human reads.

Does the list explain the attractors? The listshape headline said 'not most'. The checker found that list-structure edits alone remove an optimistic 37-60% (most of it for Gemma). The real Opus re-prompt (V1) moved F only from 32 to 25 of 40. The bound and the re-prompt disagree in size, and Qwen/Gemma were never re-prompted.

Is V2 blunt or discriminating? Round 2 scoring: it cuts right and false at the same rate. The builder's post-hoc split: it keeps 1 of 15 non-template false against 19 of 60 right. n=15, found after the fact.
Queue against per-report rules: the pilot said 'much better'; the checker says equal at under about 1,000 read and better only in reach (200-300 found at about 2% precision).

Drift: the queue's '5x more reading in 2026' was mostly in-sample optimism (unfitted rules move 1.0-1.3x). Gemma's false-alarm rate shift (136 to 219 per 10,000) is real. Errormemory's 'freshness' effect is one 2025 pump template, not general drift.
Report weighting: rawstream said per-report counting makes the LLMs look worse; the checker's ratio estimator gives the same or lower false counts.

Encoder gate: it holds 305 of 552 rare reports and costs little in the queue up to 6,600 read (and the gated pooled queue needs fewer reports for 200: 5,902 vs 7,023), yet it holds only 9 of 40 Opus false answers, so it does not stratify LLM errors.

Counting tracking new habits: quant said the Security rise was tracked about 5x; the checker found Opus's whole-year group output rose about 24x (with sampled false answers) and Gemma's about 13x, against a true 5.5x.
Filing-memory veto cost: 6-7% of right answers on 2026 but 15-21% on the 2025 tuning year.

errors: 'Every tested fix still leaves 6.7 to 47 false rare answers for each right one' and the dead-list line 'best is about 6.7x false per right' are wrong at the low end. The known Qwen prior correction is 27 right / 3 false. The encoder alone is 32 / 166 (5.2x). Round 1's best Opus rule is 58 / 380 (6.55x). The low-recall options (Qwen prior correction, encoder) break the claimed floor. Their false sides rest on 0-1 sampled rows, so they are unresolved rather than refuted, but they cannot be left out.

Direction 6 says the missing codes 'grow inside the year'. Computer System Security 16->88, Power Conditioning 5->34 and Biofilm 2->18 are 2025->2026 year-over-year changes, not growth within 2026. Two of the three are also not 'out of reach': Opus zero-shot names Computer System Security right 20 times and Biofilm 9 times in 2026.

Direction 6 (and is_it_the_problem) tie 'no prompt recovers them (RM 2 of 30)' to the 333 reports that all 7 answers miss. RM was drawn from the 398 reports that Opus zero-shot misses, one per code, round-robin. That is a different set from the 333. The 2 recoveries also occur in V0, so the scorer calls them agent drift, not a variant effect.

Direction 1's evidence attributes the veto's pump-template misses to 'cosine 0.17-0.35 to 2024'. The deployed veto uses 2024+2025 memory, where these rows reach 0.31-0.54. The 5 Failure to Reset rows it keeps are the ones still under 0.4 in the 2025 pool. The 0.17-0.35 figure explains the 2024-only-memory gap, not the misses.

An open contradiction says the encoder gate 'holds only 9 of 40 Opus false answers, so it does not stratify LLM errors'. The gate flags about 7% of reports, keeps 123 of 154 Opus right rare answers and only 9 of 40 sampled false. That is strong separation of right from false. The sentence reverses the finding.

is_it_the_problem says a Prophylactic list artefact 'dominates' for Qwen and Gemma (43 of 163, 64 of 141). For Qwen, 43/163 is 26% and the 'other' group (74) is larger. The counts also pool the 2025 and 2026 uniform rows rather than describing 2026. The checker adds that the recall trigger barely holds for Gemma.
overclaims: V5 '155 / 1,833' is listed next to the stored-output results (veto 143/2,874, rule 94/873) as if comparable. It is agent-batched coding of 233 items. V0 alone already cuts the stored 6,665 to 5,332. The 1,833 is 6,665 x 11/40 on the 40 F items, 25 of which are the two templates that notes 7 and 9 target. The 0/99 on U leaves the false side's upper bound at about 26,000 a year. The 155 right is the RR share scaled from a round-robin-by-code sample plus 2 RM 'recoveries' that the scorer calls drift.

V5 is presented as 'not unavoidable' evidence and as the basis for direction 1 ('notes built from 2024/2025 only'). The notes were written by an agent working after round 1, which had already named these exact two templates from 2026 data. The scorer and preparer both say selection influence cannot be ruled out. On the 18 non-template F items, V5 does no better than V0 (11 vs 9 still rare).

V2 sits in the dead list as 'suppresses right and false alike', yet direction 8 builds on V2+V5. On the 18 non-template F items, V2 is the only variant with a significant paired effect (0 vs 8, p=0.008), against a 62% cut on RR. 'Dead' is premature, and the synthesis contradicts itself.

'Raw LLM output counts as a new-habit alarm' is called dead, but it was never tested as proposed. That needs full-year runs and non-attractor screens. Gemma tracked the direction of the Security rise with 0 sampled false. The checker's point was overshoot in size, not that the signal is absent.

'(4,500 with an equally pre-set variant)' and direction 2's kill criterion treat noatt as a baseline. noatt was built and scored by the checker on 2026 after seeing that lr_full's attractor feature hurt there. Picking it is hindsight, even if its specification could have been fixed in advance.

Direction 7 calls the template families 'single-manufacturer'. Manufacturer fields exist only for 2024, and the round 2 sources disagree: the listshape lead says 'MiniMed', while round 1 readers and the notes say 'Tandem'. This was not measured.

Direction 4's key evidence cannot be found in any round 1 or round 2 output file: the flag covering 2.6-3.4% of ordinary reports, holding 35/40 and 28/35 Opus false answers and 84/92 and 105/109 right ones, plus the 0.6 s / 1.0 s timings and the $7-25 cost. A grep of wf1/wf2 finds no 28-of-35, 84-of-92 or 105-of-109. It appears to be the synthesiser's own unlogged computation, yet it carries a ranked direction.
missing: Rawstream shows that 'Prophylactic removal' is a real code: 11, 83 and 93 reports in 2024-2026, about 50 single-code in 2026, many from an insufflation-sensor template. Treating it purely as a list artefact to remove (leads, direction 8) ignores that removal costs these true reports. V1 already lost 2 RR Prophylactic items to the abstain terms.

Retrieval as an existing partial fix. Listshape shows that retrieval removes nearly every attractor except Opus's High Impedance (Prophylactic 119->10, Pacing Inadequately 70->4, Failure to Reset 16->2 for Qwen), and retrieval alone already gives 2,235-3,026 false. The synthesis never weighs retrieval in its 'what solves it'.

Rawstream finds that an exact-text memory-first step overwrites 47 of the 103 rare reports it answers with a non-rare code. It also finds that report-weighted accuracy flips the encoder vs LLM picture (0.805 vs 0.369) through four heavily copied Abbott glucose templates. The choice of unit (narrative vs report) matters for any deployed pipeline and is not mentioned.
V1 placed top-level abstain or restored labels on 13 of 100 ordinary reports (about 84,000 a year at 6,453 per item). That is a new class of wrong answers, not just 'changed little'.

The quant reframing is not addressed head-on: the filed code is a free database field, so per-report rare labelling of MAUDE has no user unless codes are missing or untrusted. The 'better problem' paragraph should start from this.

No prompt-test answer is replicated. V0 drifts from the stored answers on 22% of items, and no V0 re-run measures the agent's own test-retest noise. All V1/V2/V5 effects other than the template conversions are within that drift.

The queue's 'found' count assumes a reader recognises the filed rare code. The near-synonym reading of the top false positives rests on 8 agent-judged rows, and the checker lists several that are not near-synonyms. The synthesis promotes the queue to 'high confidence' without carrying this caveat.
critic.verdict: The two rounds support a narrow core. Base-rate arithmetic makes per-report rare labels from these coders mostly false on ordinary reports. Two manufacturer templates and one list artefact carry a large share of the false volume. A ranked queue reaches 200-300 rare reports at roughly 7k-25k read and about 2% precision, which is better reach than the encoder alone. Recall is capped near 219-297 of 552. The synthesis overstates the convention-note result (V5): it rests on 25 targeted template items, agent coding that already drifts 22%, and an ordinary-report false bound of about 26,000 a year. It also states a 'nothing beats 6.7x' floor that the encoder and the Qwen prior correction already break. A few direction-level facts are mis-sourced or unlogged: the 'inside the year' habit growth, the RM vs 333 conflation, the reversed reading of the encoder gate, and the direction 4 flag numbers. Read the directions as hypotheses whose first test should be the cheap CPU ones on full uniform rows (mined convention rules, cross-fitted queue), plus a human calibration read. The human read matters because whether the template 'errors' are errors at all is still open.
critic.weakest_link: The V5 convention-notes result. Three conclusions lean on it: the 'not unavoidable' argument, direction 1 and the V2+V5 plan. Yet it comes from 40 F items, 25 of them the two templates the notes were written to fix, coded by batched agents that drift 22% from the stored coder. The 0/99 ordinary-report check bounds new false answers only below about 23,000-26,000 a year.
